# Atomization brief (shared by every Flint ingest agent)

Read this whole file before writing anything. It holds the rules the Harries review taught (2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes). The review gate will check every rule here.

## Schema

Follow `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book\SKILL.md` exactly: `_domain.md`, `_book.md` (map and resume checkpoint, updated after EACH chapter or unit), and entries named `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md` with kind one of principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim. Use the frontmatter keys exactly as the skill gives them. The body has **What it is** / **Why it works** / **When to apply** / **When NOT to apply** (mandatory, non-trivial) / **Example** / **Related**.

Style reference, read before writing: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer\case-study--isometric-sprinter-and-hurdler.md`, plus one principle file in the same folder.

## Voices: label every one

- **The source author's statements are plain text.**
- **Eric's views** (from `docs/method-baseline.md` or his reviews) are prefixed "Eric's baseline:" or "Eric's review:".
- **Your own reasoning, application or synthesis** is prefixed "Inference:".
- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.

## Lessons from the Supertraining Chapter 1 review (2026-09-26: 30 FIX, 1 NO-GO of 41)

- **Keep the source's internal contradictions.** When a book says X on one page and not-X on another, record both with their pages and set `contested`. Never pick one side silently. The NO-GO entry reversed the book's SJ-CMJ strength-deficit rule because the book states it both ways.
- **Name the right voice.** In co-authored books, write "the authors" unless a passage clearly belongs to one author. A passage that names Verkhoshansky in the third person is Siff writing.
- **Keep `proven` rare and scoped.** Scope it to the replicated core (for example, "Hill's force-velocity curve"), never the whole entry, and mark any disputed sentence inside it. Four of eight `proven` ratings were lowered.
- **No mechanism the source does not give.** About a dozen "Why it works" sections supplied physiology the book never states. Label it "Inference:" or leave it out.
- **Do not add "well established" or "modern research shows" without a citation.** Name the paper, or delete the phrase.

## Lessons from the 2026-09-27 review wave (Supertraining Ch2-3, Issurin Ch3, Bondarchuk, Evans, Old Bull)

- **Invented Examples are the most common failure.** 34 of 36 Supertraining Ch2-3a Examples were unlabelled inventions. Use the source's own example where it gives one; otherwise start the Example with "Inference:".
- **"Verified against the page image" means you opened the image.** Four Issurin Ch3 entries claimed it for figures they had misread (Fig 3.7 inverted, a Table 3.7 row swapped). Sparse slides are not "bare diagrams" until you have looked.
- **Name the population and method the source gives.** Bondarchuk's data are 7,000+ native and foreign athletes, questionnaires, r >= 0.349, steroid-free; entries that said "Soviet athletes" were wrong everywhere.
- **Check what a cited paper actually says.** Issurin 2016's critique targets Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model, not Issurin's A-T-R; Herzog & Leonard 2000 shows force enhancement, against the book's sentence. When the book misreports a study, record both.
- **No review history in entries.** "Prior version", "corrected from a NO-GO finding" and similar belong in `staging/fixes_*_applied.md`, never in the entry body.
- **Fix logs must match the files.** One fixer log claimed fixes that were not made. Fixers run their own grep checks and paste the output.
- **Section headers use the vault form** `**What it is** —` (with the em dash). Do not add suffixes such as ": mandatory". Em dashes are banned only in titles and body text. Never wrap a `[[wikilink]]` across lines.

## Evidence

- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.
- Never invent a number. Keep ambiguity visible: mark unclear audio or OCR as unclear, and do not harmonize two conflicting numbers from the source; record both with their locators.
- OCR sources (`staging/ocr/*.md`): pages listed as low_confidence in the header must be checked against the page image before any number from them is cited. Use the Read tool on the PDF page, or render it.
- **OCR confidence scores miss the worst errors** (checked 2026-09-27). Zatsiorsky 2e: the OCR interleaves the two columns and the sidebars line by line, so its text is not readable prose; use it only to find content, and read and quote from the page image. *CFTS*: single-column prose that mostly reads in order, but upside-down lines come out as gibberish, some lines are dropped, and figures are scrambled, all at "0 low-confidence pages". For any OCR source, quote only after checking the page image, and read every figure and table from the image.

## Confidence

- Practitioner courses and lectures: ceiling `supported`.
- Books: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics. Soviet-era or single-lab empirical findings and training prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for single cases and anecdotes. `contested` where another library source or modern evidence disagrees (say which).

## Dedup and converge

Before each entry, grep `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library` and the staging library (`C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\library`) for the concept. If it is covered, add a new entry only for a genuinely new angle, and link the existing one in Related. List reciprocal-link suggestions in your final report. Never edit files in the vault or another agent's staging folder.

## Baylor context

Read `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\docs\method-baseline.md` (approved). Use it in When to apply, labelled "Eric's baseline:". Department names: Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, Applied Performance. Plain style, no em dashes. Use commas, colons and parentheses.

## Scope and output

- Write ONLY into your assigned staging folder. No git, no vault edits.
- Stop at a chapter or unit boundary. It is better to finish fewer chapters well; the `_book.md` checkpoint lets the next batch resume.
- Final reply: entries by kind and by confidence; chapters or units done and pending with page ranges; reciprocal-link suggestions; unclear or contradictory spots in the source; anything you could not read.
You are an independent reviewer in Flint's ingest review gate. Another model wrote these entries; your job is to FALSIFY them, not confirm. Read-only on entries and sources. Write only your report file.

Standards: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\docs\ATOMIZE_BRIEF.md` (read it first). Every rule there is a check.

For EVERY entry in scope:
1. Every number, definition, table value and quote appears at the cited PDF page (and printed page) and means the same thing. Open the pages yourself; do not trust the entry.
2. Attribution: plain text is the book author's own statement. Anything else must be labelled "Eric's baseline:", "Eric's review:" or "Inference:". Flag any unlabelled claim the author did not make, any "why it works" mechanism the author did not give, and any invented example.
3. Confidence: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics, so challenge every `proven`. Soviet-era or single-lab findings and prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for anecdotes. `contested` needs a stated reason.
4. "When NOT to apply" is present and substantive.
5. Duplicates: flag any entry that restates an existing vault entry (grep `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library`) without a new angle.
6. Missing: up to 5 important ideas in the covered pages that no entry captures.

Output (Markdown): a table with one row per entry: file | verdict (GO / FIX / NO-GO) | problem, quoting the entry and the source with its page | exact correction. For GO rows, list what you checked ("checked: 2.5x at PDF 23 / p.12"). Then the missing list. Then an overall verdict: PROMOTE, GO AFTER FIXES (list them), or NO-GO.
# Review: Supertraining 4.2 intro and 4.2.1-4.2.3 (round 1, Opus)

Reviewer: Claude Opus, independent round-1 reviewer, 2026-09-27. Read-only on the entries and sources.
Source: `staging/books/supertraining-6th-expanded.pdf`. Locators below are 0-based PDF idx = printed + 11 (viewer = idx + 1). I read the text layer for idx 218-235 and opened every figure as a page image: Fig 4.2 and 4.3 (idx 228 / p.217), Fig 4.6 (idx 231 / p.220), Fig 4.7 (idx 232 / p.221), Fig 4.8a and b (idx 233 / p.222), Fig 4.9 and 4.10 (idx 234 / p.223), with zoomed crops of 4.2, 4.3, 4.7, 4.8, 4.9 and 4.10.
Scope: the 15 files in `_scope_supertraining_ch4-2a.txt`.

## Batch-wide problems (each one is also listed in the rows)

A. **Wrong PDF locators in six entries.** The power, inertial, two-force, depth-jump, thrown-load and kinetic-framework entries give "PDF pp." equal to the printed page. The PDF page is printed + 11. Correct values are given in each row.
B. **Figures described as "verified against the page image" but misread.** Fig 4.7, Fig 4.8a and Fig 4.8b are described wrongly (see the depth-jump and thrown-load rows). The 09-27 lesson applies: a figure is "verified" only when the description matches the image.
C. **Internal contradictions in the source that were not recorded.** Reding's agonist/antagonist sequencing (p.209 vs p.215), Kots/ES "established" (p.208) vs "continue to disagree" (p.209), Fmax past 1.15 m "diminishes sharply" vs "stabilise" (p.222), Fig 4.3 caption "leg-press" vs text "seated leg extensions", and Fig 4.8a vs its text summary.
D. **Unlabelled writer's mechanisms and prescriptions.** Several "Why it works" and "When to apply" sections, listed per row.
E. **Safety claims.** The book's explicit ES safety rules on idx 225 / p.214 appear in no entry. These are: MICS "generally entirely safe" anywhere; "Under no circumstances should MACS be applied across the brain"; "not advisable to apply any form of ES to epileptics, pregnant women, cardiac patients or persons with heart pacemakers". The MICS safety claim ("cannot produce overtraining or injury", p.215) is quoted, but no entry says that the book gives no safety data for it.

ES "is generally of greater importance [for restoration] than as a means of stressing the muscles", using very-low-current devices at 0.5-8 Hz locally, transcranially or at acupuncture points (Siff & Yessis 1992).      2	type: library-entry
     3	kind: case-study
     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
     6	chapter: "4.2.1"
     7	topic: elite weightlifter electrostimulation protocol
     8	category: [electrostimulation, case-study, weightlifting]

    11	created: 2026-09-27
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Case Study: Siff's Account of Serge Reding's Electrostimulation Protocol
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors describe (p.209, third person) Serge Reding, the top Belgian
    17	superheavyweight weightlifter, "who had close training contact with one of the authors
    18	(Siff) while he stayed with him in South Africa in the early 1970s" (citing Siff, 1973). On
    19	p.215 Siff writes of "the ES training applied to the author by Serge Reding". Reding's
    20	post-session electrostimulation (ES) protocol differed significantly from Kots's (see
    21	[[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]]): after training sessions
    22	he used 0.5 to 2 second, very high intensity contractions with 10 to 15 second rest
    23	periods, for a total of 5 minutes per major muscle group, "with agonists and antagonists of
    24	each limb alternately stimulated in ipsilateral and contralateral sequences" (p.209). Reding
    25	always concluded his sessions with a few repetitions (1-3) of a long-duration (10-15 second),
    26	fairly intense tetanic contraction to serve as a type of deep massage, followed by about
    27	10-15 minutes of microcurrent stimulation (less than 200 microamps) applied across the head
    28	and spinal cord with another electrostimulator (p.209). On p.215 the stimulator is named as a
    29	Myogen Parametric stimulator "designed to offer external stimulation which in no way
    30	simulated the most frequently occurring movements of Olympic lifting", so that ES served as
    31	a form of General Physical Preparation (GPP). "The intensity of the ES was carefully
    32	periodised into the entire training programme alongside other key methods of strength
    33	training", and sessions "were always terminated with brief, deep ES muscle massage and
    34	restorative microstimulation across the brain and along the length of the spinal cord"
    35	(p.215). Reding "stressed the importance of different waveforms and regimes of FES for
    36	different categories of sport, adding that the method shared by Kots with Canadian coaches
    37	was only one of many possibilities" (p.215).
    38	
    39	The book describes the stimulation pattern two ways. p.209: agonists and antagonists of each
    40	limb alternately stimulated, ipsilateral and contralateral. p.215: "The Reding machine
    41	applied brief intense pulses alternately in a flip-flop fashion to opposite sides of the
    42	body, though not to paired agonists and antagonists." Both are recorded; the book does not
    43	reconcile them. (PDF p. 220, printed p. 209, "4.2.1.1"; PDF p. 226, printed p. 215, "4.2.1.6
    44	The Use of Electrostimulation in Training.")
    45	
    46	**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for why this dosing pattern (brief,
    47	high-intensity contractions; alternating stimulation; a closing deep-massage-style tetanic
    48	contraction; low-current cranial-spinal microstimulation) would produce a training effect.
    49	The passage is a descriptive account of practice, not an experiment.
    50	
    51	**When to apply** — Inference: use this as a documented example that elite-level ES
    52	protocols in this era varied substantially among people using the same broad technology; it
    53	is not evidence that Reding's protocol outperformed Kots's, only that it existed and was
    54	applied to a top-level athlete, with Siff as the subject (p.215).
    55	
    56	**When NOT to apply** — Untested: this is a single account, received by Siff as the subject
    57	(p.215) and described from Reding's own practice (p.209), with no reported outcome data (no
    58	before/after strength numbers), no control condition, and no independent replication in the
    59	text. The book's own two descriptions of the stimulation pattern disagree (see above). Do not
    60	treat the specific timings (0.5-2 s contractions, 10-15 s rest, 5 min per muscle group,
    61	10-15 min microcurrent under 200 microamps, p.209) as a validated prescription.
    62	
    63	**Example** — The book's own example is this case itself: Reding's protocol, received by
    64	Siff as the subject (p.215) and described from Reding's own practice (p.209). No further
    65	example is added here.
    66	
    67	**Related** — [[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]],
    68	[[claim--ratov-functional-electrostimulation-emg-triggered-sport-specific]] (a different,
    69	contemporaneous Soviet approach that Siff also witnessed).

    13	
    14	# Kots's 20%+ Electrostimulation Strength Claims Aroused American Interest; the Book Reports Failed Canadian Duplication and Continuing Disagreement
    15	
    16	**What it is** — "American interest in electrostimulation as a training adjunct was aroused
    17	in 1971, when Kots in Russia reported increases of more than 20% in muscle strength, speed
    18	and power produced by several weeks of electrotraining." The Canadians could not first
    19	produce comparable results: "Unable to produce comparable results, the Canadians invited him
    20	to lecture at Concordia University in 1977." Armed with the information that Kots employed a
    21	sinusoidally modulated 2500 Hz current source applied in a sequence of 10 seconds of
    22	contraction followed by 50 seconds of relaxation, "they again tried to duplicate Russian
    23	claims." The book does not report that outcome (PDF p. 220, printed p. 209). It gives no rep
    24	or set count for Kots's protocol.
    25	
    26	The same section states both sides of the strength question. Russian studies "have
    27	established that electrostimulation of muscle furnishes an adequate training stimulus for
    28	effective development of muscular strength (Kots, 1971; Kots & Khvilon, 1971; Khvilon,
    29	1974)" (PDF p. 219, printed p. 208). Yet, despite the success various track coaches reported
    30	in integrating conventional faradic ES into a carefully periodised programme (Francis, 1982),
    31	"researchers continue to disagree on increase in muscle strength" (PDF p. 220, printed
    32	p. 209). The clinical-effects list also names Kots & Chwilon (1971) among the sources for ES
    33	appearing "to increase the strength of competitive athletes in some instances" with
    34	periodised exercise (PDF p. 222, printed p. 211). `contested` is set for this internal
    35	disagreement. (PDF pp. 219-220, printed pp. 208-209, "4.2.1 Electrostimulation" and
    36	"4.2.1.1 The Physiological Effects of Electrostimulation.")
    37	
    38	**Why it works** — The authors give no physiological mechanism for why Kots's protocol
    39	(2500 Hz, 10 s on, 50 s off) would or would not replicate. The later "Reasons for
    40	Conflicting Research" subsection (see
    41	[[heuristic--nine-reasons-electrostimulation-research-conflicts]]) gives general
    42	methodological reasons ES research disagrees, without resolving the Kots case.
    43	
    44	**When to apply** — Inference: treat any single large ES strength-gain percentage (here,
    45	"more than 20%") as a claim tied to one fully specified protocol (waveform, frequency, duty
    46	cycle) from one lab, not a property of "electrostimulation" as a category. The Canadians
    47	could not first produce comparable results; after obtaining Kots's parameters they "again
    48	tried to duplicate" the claims, and the book does not report that outcome (p.209).
    49	Inference: the book's account therefore does not show the claims were replicated.
    50	
    51	**When NOT to apply** — This is a single historical claim and one reported duplication
    52	effort from the 1970s, with no outcome given and no independent modern confirmation in this
    53	text. Do not cite "more than 20%" as an expected or typical ES strength gain. Do not cite the
    54	book as showing that the claims were replicated or refuted: it states both "have
    55	established" (p.208) and "continue to disagree" (p.209).
    56	
    57	**Example** — Inference: a strength coach weighing NMES for a rehabilitating athlete should
    58	ask what waveform, frequency and duty cycle a cited study used. The page gives three facts
    59	for Kots's case: the Canadians could not produce comparable results, invited Kots to
    60	Concordia in 1977, and, armed with his parameters, tried again; the outcome is not reported
    61	(p.209).
    62	
    63	**Related** — [[heuristic--nine-reasons-electrostimulation-research-conflicts]],
    64	[[case-study--reding-electrostimulation-protocol-siff-account]] (a contemporaneous,
    65	differently designed elite-athlete ES protocol the authors set against the Kots/Canadian
    66	history), [[claim--strength-detraining-and-retention-timelines]] (Khvilon 1974 ES strength
    67	retention).

    13	
    14	# Nine Reasons Electrostimulation Strength Research Disagrees: A Checklist for Reading It
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors give nine specific methodological reasons why published
    17	electrostimulation (ES) strength-training studies contradict one another: (1) many studies
    18	measure only isometric or isokinetic strength change and neglect power, speed, muscular
    19	endurance, residual muscle tension, muscle growth and rate of neuromuscular recovery; (2)
    20	much research uses injured or rehabilitating patients, untrained individuals, or trained
    21	subjects of differing backgrounds, and strength gains are proportionately larger early in
    22	training or in untrained subjects, with early gains driven mainly by neuromuscular
    23	adaptation and learning rather than hypertrophy; (3) ES effectiveness depends on current
    24	intensity and individual tolerance of discomfort, and no waveform has been found to be
    25	universally most comfortable, with considerable inter-subject variation (Delitto & Rose,
    26	1986; Mannheimer & Carlsson, 1979; Moreno-Aranda & Seirig, 1981); (4) effects depend on
    27	waveform type and frequency, since slow-twitch and fast-twitch fibres have distinct
    28	recruitment patterns and functional characteristics (Lloyd et al, 1986; Mannheimer &
    29	Carlsson, 1979; Pette & Vrbova, 1985), and higher frequency (especially with a carrier
    30	wave) lowers electrode-skin impedance and raises comfort; (5) electrode type, size, number,
    31	location and gel affect delivered energy, resultant contraction force and comfort, and many
    32	studies omit these details, and "therefore, valid comparisons largely are meaningless"; (6) most
    33	studies use commercial stimulators that vary only a few of the many possible stimulation
    34	parameters (frequency, waveform, pulse-width, modulation type, impulse interval, energy
    35	delivered), so no single study has examined the full parameter space, even in the more
    36	extensive review by Lloyd et al (1986); (7) ES effects, like plyometric training, "may be
    37	enhanced by optimal integration into an overall strength and sport specific training
    38	programme (e.g. Francis, 1982)"; (8) many training regimes are deficiently designed: the
    39	stimulator is usually "selected according to the maximum tolerated by subjects", or to a
    40	percentage of a maximal voluntary isometric or isokinetic contraction, yet "subjects can
    41	withstand greater intensities of electric current from the start to end of any session, and
    42	from week to week"; ES intensity set at a fixed value, like weight training at a fixed
    43	percentage of a rising 1RM, ignores gradual overload; (9) the design and effects of a
    44	stimulator depend on the choice of physiological model. The authors state that all
    45	faradic, medium-frequency and interferential stimulators (including sports-oriented
    46	machines) are designed on the action-potential model and so cannot serve applications that
    47	rely on the other models (p.210). The alternative models the authors cite include Becker's
    48	glial-semiconductor proposal (glial cell potentials modulating nerve cells "similar to

    14	# Seventeen Claimed Clinical and Physiological Effects of Electrostimulation, With Their Original Citations
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors catalog electrostimulation's (ES) reported applications and
    17	effects, each with cited sources: (1) increase in muscle strength, greatest in the weakest
    18	or most unfit subjects, with ES alone at best producing gains "similar to or smaller than
    19	those of voluntary exercise", though with periodised exercise programmes ES "appears to
    20	increase the strength of competitive athletes in some instances" (Francis, 1982; Kots &
    21	Chwilon, 1971; Matteson, 1984; Reding, 1973), "although these changes may have been the
    22	indirect result of some of the other effects of ES" (PDF p. 222, printed p. 211); (2)
    23	re-education of faulty muscle-action patterns, e.g. chondromalacia patellae, tennis elbow,
    24	"frozen shoulder" (Eriksson, 1981; Godfrey et al, 1979; Johnson et al, 1977; Nirschl &
    25	Sobel, 1981); (3) facilitation of contraction when voluntary contraction is blocked by
    26	disuse, pain or injury, reducing tissue wasting; (4) increased muscular and systemic
    27	endurance from prolonged sub-maximal ES, with low-frequency (under 15 Hz), long-duration
    28	(24-hour) continuous stimulation or cross-innervation shown in animal studies to shift
    29	fast-twitch fibres toward a more aerobic, fatigue-resistant profile (Jolesz & Sreter, 1981;
    30	Pette, 1984; Pette & Vrbova, 1985; Salmons & Vrbova, 1969; Salmons & Henriksson, 1981); (5)
    31	increased speed of contraction from long-term, higher-frequency (over 40 Hz) ES, improving
    32	reaction time and decreasing time-to-peak-tension of fast-twitch muscles (Fleury & Lagasse,
    33	1979; Salmons & Vrbova, 1967, 1969); (6) increased local blood supply, with measured
    34	increases from about 20% to over 200%, particularly below roughly 30 Hz (Currier et al,
    35	1986; Richardson, 1981; Wakim et al, 1948; Wakim, 1953) (PDF p. 222, printed p. 211); (7) a
    36	massage-like pumping action on venous and lymphatic return; (8) pain relief via TENS, with
    37	conventional TENS at low frequency (50-100 Hz) without contraction, and modes for deeper pain
    38	using short, high-intensity bursts at 1-150 Hz with contraction (PDF p. 223, printed p. 212);
    39	(9) reduction of protective muscle spasm and spasticity; (10) promotion of relaxation and
    40	recuperation, attributed to central endorphin/enkephalin release, used by Russian athletes
    41	for post-training recuperation and to aid sleep onset even with mild thigh-only stimulation;
    42	(11) increased range of movement, used alongside PNF mobilisation; (12) reduction of
    43	non-infectious swelling (Wadsworth & Chanmugam, 1980, the single citation); (13) halting or
    44	slowing mild to moderate scoliotic curvature with ES applied to specific back muscles
    45	(Axelgaard et al, 1983; Friedman et al, 1982; Kots & Chwilon, 1971; Schultz et al, 1981);
    46	(14) preferential recruitment of the largest-diameter axons first, "the reverse of the
    47	natural order of recruitment", so ES may play a supplementary role for axons that are hard
    48	to activate in normal training (Enoka, 1988); (15) an acute strength increase after a single
    49	session: Alon (1985), studying 14 subjects, found one experimental ES session produced a mean
    50	increase in quadriceps strength of about 13% (PDF p. 223, printed p. 212); (16) improved
    51	metabolic economy: Ratov & Kryazhev (1986): quadriceps ES during cycling and speed skating
    52	cut oxygen consumption 10-17% and extended time to fatigue 15-20%. Uncited "similar
    53	research": ES during treadmill running cut oxygen consumption about 10%, and when the work
    54	was done by muscles electrically stimulated shortly before, energy consumption fell about 5%
    55	(PDF p. 224, printed p. 213); (17) increased contractile speed of skeletal muscle via
    56	phasic-type ES (Karba et al, 1990). (PDF pp. 221-224, printed pp. 210-213, "4.2.1.3 Clinical
    57	Applications of Electrostimulation.")
    58	
    59	**Why it works** — The authors give a mechanism for some items (for example 6, 9, 10, 12)
    60	and none for others (1, 3, 5, 13, 15, 16). Inference: the groupings below are the writer's.
    61	Items 4-5, 14 and 17 relate to fibre-type recruitment and conversion; items 6-13 relate to
    62	blood flow, central neurochemistry or mechanical pumping action. Inference: no single theory
    63	in this passage ties all seventeen together; the authors' own attempt at unification is the
    64	separate MACS/MICS theory (see [[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]]).
    65

    67	specific, narrow purpose (e.g. swelling reduction, pain relief, post-training recuperation).
    68	The authors write that ES "is generally of greater importance" as a means of restoration
    69	"than as a means of stressing the muscles", and that it is "unfortunate that its value has
    70	been assessed largely in terms of its direct and often contradictory effects on isometric or
    71	isokinetic strength" (PDF p. 225, printed p. 214; see also
    72	[[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]]). Inference: for Athletic
    73	Medicine or Applied Performance settings, items 6-13 (blood flow, pain, spasm, swelling,
    74	recuperation, ROM) map most directly onto standard rehabilitation and recovery use cases,
    75	while items 1-5 and 14-17 (strength, endurance, speed, recruitment, metabolic economy) are the
    76	performance-training claims.

    79	studies or small samples (e.g. Alon's 13% figure is from 14 subjects, one session); none are
    80	independently re-validated within this ingest. Item 4's fibre-type conversion evidence is
    81	from animal studies (cross-innervation, continuous 24-hour stimulation), not directly

    94	justify ES as a primary strength-training tool (item 1); a practitioner should not conflate
    95	the two when deciding whether to add ES to a programme, and should weigh item 10 against the
    96	Dupuy et al 2018 pooled result above.

    14	# Case Study: Siff's Account of Serge Reding's Electrostimulation Protocol
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors describe (p.209, third person) Serge Reding, the top Belgian
    17	superheavyweight weightlifter, "who had close training contact with one of the authors
    18	(Siff) while he stayed with him in South Africa in the early 1970s" (citing Siff, 1973). On
    19	p.215 Siff writes of "the ES training applied to the author by Serge Reding". Reding's
    20	post-session electrostimulation (ES) protocol differed significantly from Kots's (see
    21	[[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]]): after training sessions
    22	he used 0.5 to 2 second, very high intensity contractions with 10 to 15 second rest
    23	periods, for a total of 5 minutes per major muscle group, "with agonists and antagonists of
    24	each limb alternately stimulated in ipsilateral and contralateral sequences" (p.209). Reding
    25	always concluded his sessions with a few repetitions (1-3) of a long-duration (10-15 second),
    26	fairly intense tetanic contraction to serve as a type of deep massage, followed by about
    27	10-15 minutes of microcurrent stimulation (less than 200 microamps) applied across the head
    28	and spinal cord with another electrostimulator (p.209). On p.215 the stimulator is named as a
    29	Myogen Parametric stimulator "designed to offer external stimulation which in no way
    30	simulated the most frequently occurring movements of Olympic lifting", so that ES served as
    31	a form of General Physical Preparation (GPP). "The intensity of the ES was carefully
    32	periodised into the entire training programme alongside other key methods of strength
    33	training", and sessions "were always terminated with brief, deep ES muscle massage and
    34	restorative microstimulation across the brain and along the length of the spinal cord"
    35	(p.215). Reding "stressed the importance of different waveforms and regimes of FES for
    36	different categories of sport, adding that the method shared by Kots with Canadian coaches
    37	was only one of many possibilities" (p.215).
    38	
    39	The book describes the stimulation pattern two ways. p.209: agonists and antagonists of each
    40	limb alternately stimulated, ipsilateral and contralateral. p.215: "The Reding machine
    41	applied brief intense pulses alternately in a flip-flop fashion to opposite sides of the
    42	body, though not to paired agonists and antagonists." Both are recorded; the book does not
    43	reconcile them. (PDF p. 220, printed p. 209, "4.2.1.1"; PDF p. 226, printed p. 215, "4.2.1.6
    44	The Use of Electrostimulation in Training.")
    45	
    46	**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for why this dosing pattern (brief,
    47	high-intensity contractions; alternating stimulation; a closing deep-massage-style tetanic
    48	contraction; low-current cranial-spinal microstimulation) would produce a training effect.
    49	The passage is a descriptive account of practice, not an experiment.
    50	
    51	**When to apply** — Inference: use this as a documented example that elite-level ES
    52	protocols in this era varied substantially among people using the same broad technology; it
    53	is not evidence that Reding's protocol outperformed Kots's, only that it existed and was
    54	applied to a top-level athlete, with Siff as the subject (p.215).
    55	
    56	**When NOT to apply** — Untested: this is a single account, received by Siff as the subject
    57	(p.215) and described from Reding's own practice (p.209), with no reported outcome data (no
    58	before/after strength numbers), no control condition, and no independent replication in the
    59	text. The book's own two descriptions of the stimulation pattern disagree (see above). Do not
    60	treat the specific timings (0.5-2 s contractions, 10-15 s rest, 5 min per muscle group,
    61	10-15 min microcurrent under 200 microamps, p.209) as a validated prescription.
    62	
    63	**Example** — The book's own example is this case itself: Reding's protocol, received by
    64	Siff as the subject (p.215) and described from Reding's own practice (p.209). No further
    65	example is added here.

    20	to lecture at Concordia University in 1977." Armed with the information that Kots employed a

    23	claims." The book does not report that outcome (PDF p. 220, printed p. 209). It gives no rep
    24	or set count for Kots's protocol.
    25	
    26	The same section states both sides of the strength question. Russian studies "have
    27	established that electrostimulation of muscle furnishes an adequate training stimulus for
    28	effective development of muscular strength (Kots, 1971; Kots & Khvilon, 1971; Khvilon,
    29	1974)" (PDF p. 219, printed p. 208). Yet, despite the success various track coaches reported
    30	in integrating conventional faradic ES into a carefully periodised programme (Francis, 1982),
    31	"researchers continue to disagree on increase in muscle strength" (PDF p. 220, printed
    32	p. 209). The clinical-effects list also names Kots & Chwilon (1971) among the sources for ES
    33	appearing "to increase the strength of competitive athletes in some instances" with
    34	periodised exercise (PDF p. 222, printed p. 211). `contested` is set for this internal
    35	disagreement. (PDF pp. 219-220, printed pp. 208-209, "4.2.1 Electrostimulation" and
    36	"4.2.1.1 The Physiological Effects of Electrostimulation.")

    39	(2500 Hz, 10 s on, 50 s off) would or would not replicate. The later "Reasons for

    42	methodological reasons ES research disagrees, without resolving the Kots case.

    47	could not first produce comparable results; after obtaining Kots's parameters they "again
    48	tried to duplicate" the claims, and the book does not report that outcome (p.209).
    49	Inference: the book's account therefore does not show the claims were replicated.

    33	1979; Salmons & Vrbova, 1967, 1969); (6) increased local blood supply, with measured
    34	increases from about 20% to over 200%, particularly below roughly 30 Hz (Currier et al,
    35	1986; Richardson, 1981; Wakim et al, 1948; Wakim, 1953) (PDF p. 222, printed p. 211); (7) a
    36	massage-like pumping action on venous and lymphatic return; (8) pain relief via TENS, with
    37	conventional TENS at low frequency (50-100 Hz) without contraction, and modes for deeper pain
    38	using short, high-intensity bursts at 1-150 Hz with contraction (PDF p. 223, printed p. 212);
    39	(9) reduction of protective muscle spasm and spasticity; (10) promotion of relaxation and
    40	recuperation, attributed to central endorphin/enkephalin release, used by Russian athletes
    41	for post-training recuperation and to aid sleep onset even with mild thigh-only stimulation;
    42	(11) increased range of movement, used alongside PNF mobilisation; (12) reduction of
    43	non-infectious swelling (Wadsworth & Chanmugam, 1980, the single citation); (13) halting or
    44	slowing mild to moderate scoliotic curvature with ES applied to specific back muscles
    45	(Axelgaard et al, 1983; Friedman et al, 1982; Kots & Chwilon, 1971; Schultz et al, 1981);
    46	(14) preferential recruitment of the largest-diameter axons first, "the reverse of the
    47	natural order of recruitment", so ES may play a supplementary role for axons that are hard
    48	to activate in normal training (Enoka, 1988); (15) an acute strength increase after a single
    49	session: Alon (1985), studying 14 subjects, found one experimental ES session produced a mean
    50	increase in quadriceps strength of about 13% (PDF p. 223, printed p. 212); (16) improved
    51	metabolic economy: Ratov & Kryazhev (1986): quadriceps ES during cycling and speed skating
    52	cut oxygen consumption 10-17% and extended time to fatigue 15-20%. Uncited "similar
    53	research": ES during treadmill running cut oxygen consumption about 10%, and when the work
    54	was done by muscles electrically stimulated shortly before, energy consumption fell about 5%
    55	(PDF p. 224, printed p. 213); (17) increased contractile speed of skeletal muscle via
    56	phasic-type ES (Karba et al, 1990). (PDF pp. 221-224, printed pp. 210-213, "4.2.1.3 Clinical
    57	Applications of Electrostimulation.")
    58	
    59	**Why it works** — The authors give a mechanism for some items (for example 6, 9, 10, 12)
    60	and none for others (1, 3, 5, 13, 15, 16). Inference: the groupings below are the writer's.
    61	Items 4-5, 14 and 17 relate to fibre-type recruitment and conversion; items 6-13 relate to
    62	blood flow, central neurochemistry or mechanical pumping action. Inference: no single theory
    63	in this passage ties all seventeen together; the authors' own attempt at unification is the
    64	separate MACS/MICS theory (see [[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]]).
    65	
    66	**When to apply** — Use this as a reference catalog when deciding whether ES could serve a
    67	specific, narrow purpose (e.g. swelling reduction, pain relief, post-training recuperation).
    68	The authors write that ES "is generally of greater importance" as a means of restoration
    69	"than as a means of stressing the muscles", and that it is "unfortunate that its value has
    70	been assessed largely in terms of its direct and often contradictory effects on isometric or
    71	isokinetic strength" (PDF p. 225, printed p. 214; see also
    72	[[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]]). Inference: for Athletic
    73	Medicine or Applied Performance settings, items 6-13 (blood flow, pain, spasm, swelling,
    74	recuperation, ROM) map most directly onto standard rehabilitation and recovery use cases,
    75	while items 1-5 and 14-17 (strength, endurance, speed, recruitment, metabolic economy) are the
    76	performance-training claims.
    77	
    78	**When NOT to apply** — Each item rests on citations from roughly 1948-1990, mostly single
    79	studies or small samples (e.g. Alon's 13% figure is from 14 subjects, one session); none are
    80	independently re-validated within this ingest. Item 4's fibre-type conversion evidence is
    81	from animal studies (cross-innervation, continuous 24-hour stimulation), not directly
    82	transferable to standard clinical ES dosing. Do not treat this list as equally strong
    83	evidence across all seventeen items: blood flow and pain relief carry several citations each
    84	here, while swelling (item 12) rests on one citation and acute strength (item 15) on two.
    85	Inference: item 14's reverse-order recruitment is disputed. External: Gregory & Bickel 2005
    86	(PMID 15794706) set out the contention that electrical stimulation recruits motor units "in a
    87	nonselective, spatially fixed, and temporally synchronous pattern" (abstract read). Contrast
    88	for item 10: Dupuy et al 2018 meta-analysis found that electrostimulation did not
    89	significantly improve DOMS or fatigue in the pooled analyses (vault entry, p.11):
    90	[[research-papers/dupuy-2018-an-evidence-based-approach-for-choosing-post-exercise-recovery-techniques-to-reduce-marker]]
    91	
    92	**Example** — Inference: a post-training recovery application (item 10, mild stimulation to
    93	aid relaxation and sleep onset) is a different use case from citing this same list to
    94	justify ES as a primary strength-training tool (item 1); a practitioner should not conflate
    95	the two when deciding whether to add ES to a programme, and should weigh item 10 against the
    96	Dupuy et al 2018 pooled result above.
    97	
    98	**Related** — [[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]],
    99	[[heuristic--nine-reasons-electrostimulation-research-conflicts]],
   100	[[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]],
   101	[[claim--ratov-functional-electrostimulation-emg-triggered-sport-specific]] (item 16 is the
   102	only quantitative data from Ratov's group in this section),

3	SUPERTRAINING
4	excellent for general preparation” may then be seen to be simplistic and misleading. Virtually any training 
5	may be rendered impotent or harmful if it is administered in an inappropriate manner for a given individual 
6	given stage of his/her training career. 
7	Conversely, methods which may appear to be offer only mz 
8	improvements on their own, may in optimal combinations yield results which clearly show that “the whole 
9	greater than the sum of its parts”.
10	Steps Towards Structuring the Training Process
11	One issue is still very important for devising methods of strength training. A training effect occurs through 
12	frequent and systematic repetition of a complex of different interacting means. The training load is understood 
13	be the sum of all the specific influences on the body, its essential characteristics being:
14	• its resulting effect (the qualitative and quantitative assessment of the special work capacity of the athlete)
15	• its composition or contents (the complex of means applied)
16	• its structure (correlation of means)
17	• its volume (the quantity of the training work)
18	• its intensity (the difficulty or quality of the training work).
19	To assess the effectiveness o f the training process, it is appropriate to examine further how the composi 
20	structure, the volume and intensity of the training load relate to the resulting effect. The purpose of managing 
21	training load is to obtain a pronounced and safe training effect through the logical organisation of the com 
22	and structure of the load, by use of an optimal volume and intensity of exercise.
23	A load will prove effective if its means create an adequate training effect, i.e. evoke specific adaptation in 
24	body. This is especially important for highly qualified athletes, since the means they have used in previous staga 
25	of preparation do not elicit an adequate training effect for continued improvement. Therefore, the search 
26	highly effective means and methods of special strength training is always fundamental to scientific S| 
27	preparation. During the past few decades, isometric and isokinetic exercises have been used, as well as tht 
28	plyometric method of developing cxplosive-strength, the electrostimulation method and others. Although not 
29	of them have been studied sufficiently, and detailed methods for their use have not been determined, they 
30	appreciable success, thereby confirming their effectiveness and the research findings in this field.
31	In recent years the volume of the load has been increased significantly. However, it is impossible toaccej* 
32	the view that increase in training volume is the only or best possibility for enhancing the effectiveness of the 
33	athlete's preparation.
34	Elementary logic and practical experience clearly indicate that it is impossible for sheer quantity of w o n  
35	compensate for a low training effect of any given means. However, there is also no guarantee that highly effective 
36	specialised means, logically organised in a specific training cycle, can produce a high level of special work canac 
37	at a significantly smaller volume o f exercise and in a shorter time. Nevertheless, it should be noted that the 
38	volume of the load is undoubtedly one of the conditions for raising the special work capacity in many 
39	(chiefly the cyclic types) during specific stages of preparation.
40	In order not to create an incorrect impression about the volume of the load we must point out that it resol 
41	two basic tasks in the training process. Firstly, it provides a functional base for the further development 
42	specific work capacity. Secondly, it is associated with raising the level of special fitness, primarily by develop’ 
43	endurance. If the first task is significant as a universal training principle, then the second is appropriate only for 
44	certain types of sport. It should be added that the volume of the training work is an important condition for 
45	successful technical preparation. Besides this, research indicates that there is a direct correlation between the 
46	volume of the load and the length of time over which a training effect is maintained.
47	In addition to its volume, the structure o f the training scheme is vitally important in every sport. From 
48	practical experience it is known that no one means or method of special preparation should be consider' 
49	universal or absolutely effective. Each of them should have its own special place during a particular training stage, 
50	depending upon factors including the specificity of the sport, the athlete's level o f fitness, the character of the 
51	previous training loads, and the specific aims of the current training stage. With respect to this, research has 
52	shown clearly that special strength training using a specific system of different means and methods produces i 
53	significantly greater effect than the separate random use of different means and methods (sec Ch 6), this advantage 
54	being achieved even with a smaller volume of work (Verkhoshansky, 1966, 1970; Tatyan, 1974; Khodvkin. 
55	1975).
56	206
57	
58	######## IDX 218 (printed 207)
59	SUPERTRAINING
60	One more feature should be noted. I f the given means do not elicit an adequate training effect, then increase 
61	m work capacity becomes more a factor o f specialised exercise than training volume and then only if it is executed 
62	by training at or near personal maximum levels. It should be pointed out that the execution o f specialised 
63	exercises in training at near maximal intensity (as advocated by Bulgarian experts) should be regarded as an 
64	advanced strategy, a method which cannot be acknowledged as being universally appropriate. This would imply 
65	not only rejecting the principles of the rational structuring of training based on research into training methods, but 
66	also a return to the original concepts from which these began.
67	Thus, the problem of establishing scientifically the means of sport training is far from being solved and the 
68	current tendency to increase the volume of the training load should not detract from its significance and turn the 
69	attention of specialists away from its in-depth study.
70	If a logical sequence is to be recommended as a practical solution to the problem of improving the 
71	effectiveness of special strength training methods, then it should be laid down as follows:
72	1. Regime —
73	2. Means — ► 3. Methods — ► 4. System — ► 5. Volume
74	From this scheme it follows that the means of special strength training should be selected on the basis of 
75	quantitative descriptions of the motor specificity of the given sport and thereby provide an adequate regime of 
76	work for the body. The basic criterion for this is a guarantee of a definite training effect for the given level of 
77	special fitness.
78	The next step is to determine a suitable method of using the means based not only on the specific motor 
79	regimes of the given sport, but also on factors such as one’s level of fitness and the tasks of the current stage of 
80	training. Of great potential for perfecting the methods of special strength training, is the principle o f systematic 
81	application o f means to produce the necessary cumulative training effect.
82	Finally, attaining the necessary level of special strength training depends on the volume of the special work, 
83	the optimal magnitude of which should be determined by the stage and current tasks of the athlete's preparation, 
84	the competition calendar and the intensity of the load.
85	This scheme emphasizes that, to rely on any one parameter of the load for achieving any given potential is 
86	appropriate only after the potential of the previous parameter has been completely exploited. For example, it is 
87	unwise to increase training volume without having fully elicited the maximum training effect of the individual 
88	strength training means at a particular intensity. This requires dedication and persistence from the specialists, 
89	because it requires in-depth investigative effort Since increasing the training volume is easier than finding a really 
90	effective means of special preparation, such a course tends to be a much simpler choice.
91	4.2 Different Means of Strength Development
92	The external force generated by muscles is a result of voluntary effort. 
93	However, under normal everyday 
94	conditions, muscular tension produced by voluntary effort has certain limitations. 
95	To increase the external 
96	muscular force it is necessary to stimulate them from the outside, for example, by means of mechanical 
97	stimulation. Afferent impulses elicited by mechanical stimulation inform the central nervous system about the 
98	strength of the external influence evoking the muscular tension. The greater the intensity of the external stimulus, 
99	the greater the muscle effector discharge, and the larger the external work produced.
100	Thus, afferent signals to the neuromuscular system play an important role in determining the qualitative and 
101	quantitative characteristics of muscular strength. 
102	Therefore, the stimulation of muscular tension for the 
103	development of strength is of great significance. So, in all cases the magnitude of working muscular tension is 
104	determined by voluntary effort and external mechanical action. The stimulation of working force can be divided 
105	into the following basic types:
106	• Stimulation when muscular tension is produced by voluntary effort against external resistance, and the
107	resistance of the moving load accelerates and regulates the effector impulses to the muscles
108	• Stimulation by the kinetic energy of a falling object or the body, when the effort is primarily reflexive
109	• Stimulation caused primarily by voluntary effort, under conditions where additional external mechanical
110	stimulation is absent or limited
111	• Stimulation of muscle elicited or intensified involuntarily by means of external electrical current.
112	207
113	
114	######## IDX 219 (printed 208)
115	SUPERTRAINING
116	The first two cases are associated with dynamic work and the third with isometric work. 
117	An increase in 
118	stimulation is realised in the first case by increasing the velocity of the preliminary fall of the body or load, and by 
119	mobilising the athlete's voluntary resources in the third. It should also be pointed out that voluntary effort plays 
120	an important role in the magnitude of the effector response of the muscles in the first instance, whereas its 
121	influence in the second is insignificant.
122	The mechanism chiefly responsible for the braking or amortisation work of the muscles causes a protective 
123	effector response more rapidly than a voluntary sequence of actions. Therefore, such a reflex stimulus is able to 
124	provoke an extraordinary mobilisation of the neuromuscular apparatus, which is impossible where there is reliance 
125	on voluntary effort alone. This mechanism forms the foundation of plyometric training (5.2.4).
126	4.2.1 E lectrostim ulation
127	As has already been stated, there is always an ongoing search for novel, highly effective means of special strength 
128	training. For example, Russian studies have established that clcctrostimulation of muscle furnishes an adequate 
129	training stimulus for effective development of muscular strength (Kots, 1971; Kots & Khvilon, 1971; Khvilon, 
130	1974). Electrostimulation can be effective for certain purposes in the preparation of highly qualified athletes 
131	(mainly in speed-strength sports) and there are a number of advantages associated with this method of developing 
132	strength, in particular the reduction of joint loading. It can occupy a specific place in the yearly training cycle, be 
133	used in combination with other methods of developing muscular strength and be applied chiefly in the preparation 
134	of highly qualified athletes.
135	Ratov has found that functional electrical stimulation (FENS) can be particularly useful in improving sporting 
136	performance. His techniques, developed decades ago from his PhD programme on the interrelation between 
137	electrical stimulation and electromyography, has used EMG signals from agonist and antagonist muscles to act as 
138	triggers or control mechanisms for electrical stimulation of musclcs directly involved in producing functional 
139	movements in sport. In his laboratory at the State Central Institute for Sports Science in Moscow he has 
140	successfully implemented these neuromuscular stimulation methods in training athletes such as fencers, boxers, 
141	rowers, shotputtcrs and weightlifters.
142	However, it is inappropriate to consider the training applications of electrostimulation in detail here because 
143	its methodological fundamentals have still not been determined, especially as it should be applied preferably under 
144	suitable conditions by qualified personnel. 
145	The next section summarises the effects and applications of 
146	electrostimulation as a form of supplementary sports preparation.
147	4.2.1.1 The Physiological E ffects of Electrostim ulation
148	The concept o f elcctrostimulation is not new, and for years has been used by physical therapists in clinical 
149	applications such as muscle rehabilitation, relief of muscular spasm, reduction of swelling and pain control. Its 
150	possible value in sports training is still considered controversial. In strength conditioning, the applications of 
151	electrostimulation fall into the following broad categories:
152	• Imposition of local physical stress to provoke supercompensation
153	• Local restoration after exercise or injury
154	• General central nervous and endocrine restoration after exercise or injury
155	• Neuromuscular stimulation for pain control or movement patterning
156	Electrostimulation usually involves feeding the muscles low current electrical impulses via moistened electrode 
157	pads placed firmly on the skin. The effectiveness, comfort and depth of excitation depends on factors such as 
158	pulse shape, frequency, duration, intensity and modulation pattern. The resulting number of possible stimulation 
159	combinations immediately emphasizes how difficult it is to determine the optimum balance of variables and 
160	compare the results of different researchers.
161	The typical clinical machine supplies pulsating direct (galvanic) and/or alternating (faradic) current in the form 
162	of brief pulses. The frequency of faradic current is most commonly chosen in the range of about 50-100 Hz, while 
163	pulse duration (width) ranges from about 100 microseconds to several hundred milliseconds. This brevity of pulse 
164	duration is important to minimise skin irritation and tissue damage. However, the duration at any particular 
165	intensity of faradic stimulation should not be too brief Although they may be suitable for decreasing pain, pulses 
166	that are too brief will supply insufficient energy to cause full, tetanic muscle contraction.
167	208
168	
169	######## IDX 220 (printed 209)
170	SUPERTRAINING
171	Machines are designed to apply alternating currents directly at a preset or selected frequency (conventional 
172	faradism), or in the form of low frequency currents superimposed on a medium frequency (2000 to 5000 Hz) 
173	earner wave. A variation of the latter method, using two pairs of electrodes each supplying medium frequency 
174	waves carrying low frequency waves differing slightly in frequency, forms the basis of what is called interferential 
175	stimulation. A major advantage of using a higher frequency carrier wave is that impedance between the electrodes 
176	and skin is lowered, enhancing comfort and effectiveness.
177	American interest in electrostimuiation as a training adjunct was aroused in 1971, when Kots in Russia 
178	reported increases of more than 20% in muscle strength, speed and power produced by several weeks of 
179	dectrotraining. Unable to produce comparable results, the Canadians invited him to lecture at Concordia 
180	University in 1977. Armed with the new information that Kots employed a sinusoidally modulated 2500 Hz 
181	cunent source applied in a sequence of 10 seconds of contraction followed by 50 seconds of relaxation, they again 
182	tried to duplicate Russian claims.
183	It is noteworthy that this procedure differed significantly from that of top Belgian superheavy weightlifter. 
184	Serge Reding, who had close training contact with one of the authors (Siff) while he stayed with him In South 
185	Africa in the early 1970s. After training sessions he used 0.5 to 2 second, very high intensity contractions with 
186	10 to 15 second rest periods, for a total of 5 minutes per major muscic group, with agonists and antagonists of 
187	each limb alternately stimulated in ipsilateral and contralateral sequences (Siff, 1973). Reding always concluded 
188	his sessions with a few repetitions (1-3) of a long duration (10-15 seconds) fairly intense tetanic contraction to 
189	serve as a type o f deep massage, followed by about 10-15 minutes of microcurrent stimulation (less than 200 
190	microamps) applied across the head and spinal cord with another electrostimulator.
191	Despite the subsequent success reported by various track coaches in integrating conventional faradic 
192	electrostimulation into a carefully periodised training programme (Francis, 1982), researchers continue to disagree 
193	on increase in muscle strength.
194	4.2.1.2 Reasons for C onflicting Research
195	There are several main reasons for the contradictory research findings:
196	1. Many studies focus largely on isometric or isokinetic strength changes, which complicates research 
197	comparisons. Such research often neglects possible effects of other vital factors such as power, speed, muscular 
198	endurance, residual muscic tension, muscle growth and rate of neuromuscular recovery.
199	2. Much of the research examines injured patients in the process of rehabilitation, untrained individuals, or trained 
200	subjects from differing fitness and training backgrounds. 
201	It is well known that an increase in strength is 
202	proportionately greater in the early stages of a training programme or among untrained subjects. Moreover, 
203	increases in strength for novices during the first few weeks of training mainly are due to neuromuscular adaptation 
204	and learning, rather than muscle hypertrophy.
205	3. The effectiveness of electrostimuiation is determined by the intensity of the current used and individual 
206	tolerance of discomfort caused by stimulation. In addition, no specific waveform has been found to be universally 
207	most comfortable. There also can be considerable variation among subjects in their response to different 
208	waveforms and stimulation impedances (Delitto & Rose, 1986; Mannheimcr & Carlsson, 1979; Moreno-Aranda 
209	& Seirig, 1981).
210	4. The effects of electrostimuiation depend on the types and frequency of waveforms used, particularly since 
211	there is a distinct difference in the recruitment patterns and functional characteristics of slow-twitch and fast- 
212	twitch muscle fibres (Lloyd ct al, 1986; Mannheimer & Carlsson, 1979; Pette & Vrbova, 1985). Moreover, the 
213	higher the frequency, particularly if a carrier wave is used, the lower the impedance between electrodes and skin, 
214	and the greater the degree of comfort.
215	5. The type, size, number and location of electrodes, as well as the electrode gel, affect the amount of electrical 
216	energy transmitted to the muscles, the resultant force of contraction and patient comfort. Many studies do not 
217	discuss these details, and therefore, valid comparisons largely are meaningless.
218	6. Most studies have used commercial electrostimulators which arc able to vary only a few of all the possible 
219	stimulation parameters. Some of the more extensive studies have varied several of these parameters, as 
220	summarised in the thorough review by Lloyd et al (1986). However, because of the enormous number of

225	stimulation combinations theoretically possible, no single extensive study has been able to examine the effects of 
226	varying all the stimulation parameters. This includes frequency, waveform, pulse-width, type of modulation 
227	(Frequency Modulation, Amplitude Modulation or pulse-width modulation), impulse interval and electrical 
228	energy delivered.
229	7. The effects of electrostimulation, like plyometric training, may be enhanced by optimal integration into an 
230	overall strength and sport specific training programme (e.g. Francis, 1982)
231	8. Many of the training regimes have been deficiently designed. Usually, the electrostimulator is selected according 
232	to the maximum tolerated by subjects, or to a certain percentage of a maximal voluntary isometric or isokinetic 
233	contraction as measured on isokinetic or other dynamometers. It should be noted that adaptation to any stimulus 
234	occurs, and subjects can withstand greater intensities of electric current from the start to end of any session, and 
235	from week to week.
236	Similarly, studies examining the combined effects of electrostimulation and normal strength training often 
237	prescribe weight training with a fixed number of sets and loads at a fixed percentage of single repetition maximum, 
238	despite the fact that the latter maximum gradually increases. The accompanying electrical stimulation also is set at 
239	a fixed value, which fails to consider that the basic principle of strength and power enhancement is gradual 
240	overload. Such a training regime in normal weight training is known to be highly limited in improving physical 
241	performance. It would be surprising if it were any different with electrostimulation training.
242	9. The design and effects of the electrostimulator depend on the choice of physiological model. Most stimulators 
243	are designed on the basis of the action-potential model of nerve cell discharge, which considers that cellular 
244	communication in the body is mediated by bursts of electrical discharge transmitted along nerve axons. The cell is 
245	assumed to be W  (discharging electricity) or 'off (resting), depending on whether the build-up of electrical charge 
246	in the cell is large enough to exceed a certain threshold, rendering the cell membrane temporarily more permeable to 
247	certain chemical ions. Intermediate subthreshold states arc presumed unimportant, although they are central to an 
248	understanding of the EEG (brain waves) and other electrical potentials of the central nervous system (Siff, 1981).
249	Similarly, the numerous glial cells which surround all nerve cells are assumed to play little more than a 
250	nutritional or supportive role for the nerves, despite the fact that they display a steady or quasi-steady electric 
251	field (Galambos, 1961; Siff, 1981). Some scientists believe that glial cell potentials may have a profound effect on 
252	nerve cells by modulating their activity similar to semiconductors such as transistors in electronic circuits (Becker. 
253	1974; Galambos, 1961). In addition, the DC injury potentials measurable on the skin surface after tissue damage 
254	are not associated with the action potential system (Becker, 1982).
255	Moreover, little is known about electrical fields at the subcellular level. The sensitivity of the body to 
256	external electric, magnetic and electromagnetic fields cannot satisfactorily be explained in terms of action 
257	potentials, which are not directly affected by these fields (Becker, 1965; Cope, 1974). The classical theories also 
258	do not explain the mechanisms whereby electric and other fields stimulate processes such as the repair of 
259	fractures, the healing of wounds and reduction of thrombosis.
260	On discovering evidence for semiconduction and the possible existence of superconductivity at room 
261	temperature in biological systems, scientists now have postulated that tissue healing, pain mechanisms, cell 
262	growth and disease processes may involve biological semiconduction and superconductivity (Becker, 1965; Cope, 
263	1971; Cope, 1974). In addition, Nordenstrom claims to have shown the presence of closed electric circuits in the 
264	body, whereby ionic flow concerned with growth and regulatory processes takes place via blood vessels and 
265	through or along the capillaries (Nordenstrom, 1983).
266	All faradic, medium frequency and interferential stimulators (including sports-oriented machines) are designed 
267	on the action-potential model for cell operation, which, therefore, do not permit applications relying on the other 
268	types of models described above. Such applications involve cell growth, tissue repair and general recuperation, all 
269	of which are essential features of physical conditioning. In recent years a few innovative micro-current machines 
270	based on these models have been applied clinically with significant success in neuromuscular rehabilitation (Chee 
271	& Walton, 1986; Matteson, 1984; Matteson & Eberhardt, 185; Meyer & Nebrensky, 1983; Noto & Grant, 1985).
272	4.2.1.3 Clinical Applications of Electrostim ulation
273	At this point it is relevant to survey the clinical and research evidence supporting the value of elcctrostimulation 
274	in medical situations. Its major applications or effects are the following:

279	1. Increase in Muscle Strength
280	A wide range of low and medium frequencies has been shown to strengthen muscle tissue in the case of subjects 
281	who have been incapacitated by injury, illness or childbirth ( Eriksson, 1981; Johnson et al, 1977; Laughman et al, 
282	1983; Lloyd et al, 1986; Raitsin, 1974; Romero et al, 1982; Turk et al, 1980). Some studies on the effect of 
283	clectrostimulation (ES) alone on normal subjects also have revealed strength increases (Currier & Mann, 1983; 
284	Laughman et al, 1983: McMiken et al, 1983; Romero et al, 1982; Sekowitz, 1985), although some of these studies 
285	showed that ES was not superior to voluntary exercise (Currier & Mann, 1983; Laughmen et al, 1983; McMiken 
286	et al, 1983; Sckowitz, 1985). Further studies found minimal or insignificant changes in strength (Massey et al, 
287	1965; Mohr ct al, 1985; Singer etal, 1983).
288	In general, most of these studies indicate that ES unaccompanied by physical training at best produces long­
289	term strength gains which are similar to or smaller than those of voluntary exercise. The greatest strength increases 
290	are invariably found in the weakest or most unfit subjects (Fahey et al, 1985; Johnson et al, 1977; Romero et al, 
291	1982). However, in conjunction with periodised exercise programmes, ES appears to increase the strength of 
292	competitive athletes in some instances (Francis, 1982; Kots & Chwilon, 1971; Matteson, 1984; Reding, 1973), 
293	although these changes may have been the indirect result of some of the other effects of ES discussed below.
294	2. Re-education of Muscle Action
295	Some medical disorders or kinesiological habits may produce weak or faulty patterns of muscle action. ES may 
296	facilitate more efficient use of the affected muscles. It can be particularly effective in treating chondromalacia 
297	patellae, tennis elbow and 'frozen shoulder* (Eriksson, 1981; Godfrey et al, 1979; Johnson et al, 1977; Nirchl & 
298	Sobel, 1981).
299	3. Facilitation of Muscle Contraction
300	If one is unable to produce a voluntary muscle contraction because of disuse, pain or injury, ES can promote 
301	muscle activity and reduce the likelihood of extensive tissue wasting (Eriksson, 1981; Johnson ct al, 1977; Turk et
302	il, 1980; Vodovnik et al, 1982).
303	4. Increase of Muscular and Systemic Endurance
304	Prolonged application of sub-maximal ES can stimulate the fatiguing conditions encountered in strenuous physical 
305	work thereby increasing endurance o f the muscles involved (Ikai & Yabe, 1969; Johnson et al, 1977). Russian 
306	research reported improvement in cardiovascular efficiency, muscle contractility and rate of general recovery 
307	(Dombrovskaya, 1982). Moreover, low frequency (under 15 Hz) ES of long duration (24-hour) continuous 
308	stimulation experiments or cross-innervation experiments in animals have been shown to alter fast twitch fibres to 
309	bccome predominantly aerobic and more resistant to fatigue (Jolesz & Sreter, 1981; Pette, 1984; Pette & Vrbova, 
310	1985; Salmons & Vrbova, 1969; Salmons & Henriksson, 1981).
311	5. Increase of Speed of Muscle Contraction
312	Long-term higher frequency (more than 40 Hz) ES can improve reaction time and decrease the time to peak 
313	tension of fast twitch muscles (Fluery & Lagasse, 1979; Salmons & Vrbova, 1967, 1969).
314	6. Increase in Local Blood Supply
315	ES stimulates muscles to contract rhythmically, producing dilatation of the blood vessels, facilitating the transport 
316	of nutrients to the tissues, and possibly accelerating healing in tissues which are not extensively injured 
317	(Dombrovskaya, 1982; Salmons & Vrbova, 1967 Wadsworth & Chanmugam, 1980). Experiments using different 
318	stimulation regimes have measured increases in blood flow ranging from about 20% to more than 200%, both 
319	during and after ES, particularly if the frequencies used are below approximately 30 Hz (Currier et al, 1986; 
320	Richardson, 1981; Wakim ct al, 1948; Wakim, 1953). In general, the higher the frequency of ES, the lower the 
321	percentage increase in blood flow (Currier ct al, 1986; Wakim, 1953).
322	7. Provision of Effective Massage
323	ES increases the pumping action of muscle on the venous and lymphatic systems, which help injured, tense or 
324	fatigued areas dissipate fluid and toxin accumulation (Dombrovskaya, 1982; Wadsworth & Chanmugam, 1980). 
325	Russian studies using radioactive Xenon (Xei33) injected as a tracer confirm that massage accelerates local blood

333	ES applied by TENS (Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation) devices can relieve painful muscle spasm or 
334	tension, as well as diminish acute or chronic pain caused by a wide range of musculoskeletal conditions (Gersh & 
335	Wolf, 1985; Jeans, 1979; Lloyd et al, 1986; Mannheim & Carlsson, 1979; Sjolund & Eriksson, 1979; Strauss, 
336	1987; Wadsworth & Chanmugam, 1980). Conventional TENS employs low frequency (50 to 100 Hz) stimulation 
337	with no muscle contraction. TENS modes for management of deeper pain may use short, high intensity bursts at 
338	frequencies between 1 and 150 Hz with definite muscle contraction.

340	Protective spasm can occur in any overloaded, injured, inflamed or painful muscle. The effectiveness of ES in 
341	reducing spasm and spasticity has been attributed to one or more of the following mechanisms: promotion of 
342	muscular fatigue, disruption of the pain-spasm cycle or restoration of the normal contraction-relaxation process 
343	(Alfieri, 1982; Mills et al, 1984; Wadsworth & Chanmugam, 1980).
344	10. Prom otion of Relaxation and Recuperation
345	Short-term, intense, muscle-contracting ES and mild, non-contracting TENS-type stimulation both can promote 
346	local and general relaxation. This effect has been ascribed, in animal and human subjects, to the release in the 
347	central nervous system of endorphins and enkephalins, classes of analgesic and tranquiliser which occur naturally 
348	in the body (Gersh & Wolf, 1985; Sjolund & Eriksson, 1979). This application is used by Russian athletes in 
349	recuperating after strenuous training sessions and in facilitating the onset of sleep, even by applying mild stimu­
350	lation to the thighs alone (Dombrovskaya, 1982; Kopisov & Nagorniy, 1982).
351	11. Increase in Range of M ovem ent
352	In physical therapy, PNF (Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation) techniques often arc used to improve joint 
353	mobility caused by inactivity or injury. ES may be used in conjunction with such mobilisation techniques to 
354	enhance their effectiveness. In the case of injury, the ES may aid relaxation and mobility by diminishing pain, 
355	reducing swelling and improving microcirculation within the tissues (Wadsworth & Chanmugam, 1980).
356	12. Reduction of Swelling
357	Swelling (oedema) is the accumulation of excessive extracellular fluid in the region of a joint, arising from leakage of 
358	protein and plasma through the capillary walls of soft tissues. It may be caused by inflammation, sprains, strains, 
359	tendinitis, rheumatoid arthritis, surgery or disease. Low intensity ES can rapidly reduce swelling of non-infectious 
360	origin (Wadsworth & Chanmugam, 1980). Its effectiveness may be due to the pumping action of muscle and/or 
361	the creation o f an electric gradient across the cell membranes, which triggers the lymphatic system to absorb 
362	excess fluid.

364	Abnormal spinal curvaturc has been halted or the progress has slowed in mild to moderate scoliosis, by ES 
365	appropriately applied to specific back muscles (Axelgaard et al, 1983; Friedman et al, 1982; Kots & Chwilon, 
366	1971; Schultz etal, 1981).

374	session of ES produced a mean increase in quadriceps strength of about 13%.

390	4.2.1.4 Further Research Findings
391	Recent research and clinical experience have revealed that electric currents as much as 1000 times smaller than that 
392	of all the traditional physical therapy modalities can be far more successful than the latter in achieving many of 
393	the benefits outlined in the previous section.
394	Currents as low as 10 microamps (millionths of an amp) pulsating at between 0.1 to 400Hz are too weak to 
395	cause muscle contraction, block pain signals or cause local heating, yet their effectiveness and safety is often 
396	superior in many applications to that of faradism, interfercntialism and conventional TENS (Matteson & 
397	Eberhardt, 1985).
398	The steps to satisfactorily modify the existing paradigm for ES may be sought in the research findings quoted 
399	earlier in the section: 'Reasons for conflicting research'. There, it was learned that cellular and subcellular 
400	processes not involving cell discharge, propagated electrical impulses, or muscle contraction, appear to be 
401	involved with cellular growth and repair.
402	Some studies have produced findings which offer partial answers to the questions posed by 
403	microstimulation. For instance, work by Becker and others suggests that small, steady or slowly varying currents 
404	can cause sub-threshold modulation of the electric fields across nerve and glial cells, thereby directly regulating cell 
405	growth and communication (Becker, 1974; Becker & Marino, 1982). In this respect, some of Becker's applications 
406	included the acceleration of wound healing, partial regeneration of amphibian and rat limbs, and induction of 
407	narcosis with transcranial currents. Nordenstrom maintains that these electric currents can stimulate the flow of 
408	ions along the blood vessels and through the cell membranes which constitute the body's closed electric circuits 
409	postulated by his theory (Nordenstrom, 1983).
410	Pilla (1974) has paid particular attention to electrochemical information transfer across cell membranes. The 
411	model in this case hypothesizes that the molecular structure of the cell membrane reflects its current genetic 
412	activity. Here, the function of a cell at any instant is determined by feedback between DNA in the cell nucleus and 
413	a macromolecule inducer liberated from the membrane by means o f a protein (enzyme) regulator derived from 
414	messenger RNA activity within the cell. The activity of these membrane-bound proteins is strongly modulated by 
415	changes in the concentration of divalent ions (such as calcium Ca"^) absorbed on the membrane. ES may elicit 
416	these ionic changes and thereby modify cell function.
417	It has been shown that ES at 5Hz stimulates synthesis of DNA in chick cartilage cells and rat bone by as 
418	much as 27%, but not in chick skin fibroblasts or rat spleen lymphocytes (Rodan et al, 1978). Not only does the 
419	effect of ES appear to be tissue-specific, but the increase in DNA synthesis occurs 4-6 hours after 15 minutes of 
420	ES. The process of membrane depolarisation carried by sodium ions seems to be followed by an increase in 
421	intracellular Ca4^ concentration, thereby triggering DNA synthesis in cells susceptible to the particular stimulus. 
422	Further work by Pilla (1981) has confirmed the existence of cellular 'windows' which open most effectively to 
423	certain frequencies, pulse widths and pulse amplitudes. To attune the ES signal to these parameters, monitoring of 
424	tissue impedances is preferable, a system employed by so-called 'Intelligent TENS' devices.
425	In addition, Cheng et al (1982) have shown that stimulation with currents from 50-1000 microamps can 
426	increase tissue ATP concentrations in rats by 300-500%, and enhances amino acid transport through the cell 
427	membrane and consequent protein synthesis by as much as 40%. Interestingly, the same study reported that 
428	increasing the current above only one milliamp was sufficient to depress tissue ATP and protein synthesis - and 
429	traditional ES usually applies currents exceeding 20 milliamps, at which stage this depression being nearly 50%.
