It should also be added that the resistance, its speed of movement and the duration o f the work determine I 
how it influences which muscles produce the movement, the coordination of their actions and the instant when the 
work ceases. The most stable indicator of the coordination of muscular activity during the repetitive lifting of a 
barbell is the sequential involvement of the same specific muscles which are essential to the given movement.
In an experiment using 60% of 1RM, the muscles taking part in the work remained the same for 82% of the 
time in all athletes. With 80% of 1RM weights, the degree of consistency was less (thereby showing greater 
individuality), but was higher for qualified athletes. The coordination of muscular activity was also disrupted by ' 
fatigue (Pakhomov, 1967).
In addition, the relative contributions by the participating muscles can change during repetitive work 
(Lazareva, 1966, Kozlov, 1966). The number of muscle groups involved with a movement can either decrease 
(Moikin, 1964) or increase (Averyanov, 1963). In movements executed with little effort or low velocity a large 
part of the work involves the muscles of the body’s distal links (Tochilov, 1946; Kosilov, 1948; Vinogradov, 
1951). For movements against significant resistance or executed at high velocity, the activity characteristically 
shifts to the muscles of the proximal links, which tend to play a more tonic or postural role. These findings reveal 
that muscle isolation under conditions of significant resistance is impossible, as discussed later (4.2.9).
Thus, the factors just discussed have a profound influence on the working effect of the movement and the 
specificity of the strength developed. Therefore, when selecting strength exercises against resistance, one should 
consider these factors in accordance with the characteristics of the given sport, with particular attention being paid 
to the distinctive effects associated with the torque produced by resistance exercises. For example, in the starting 
position for the squat and squat jumps (before beginning the dynamic effort), the muscles of the legs and torso 
have already developed tension equal to the weight of the apparatus being held. On the other hand, with the 
snatch or clean-and-jerk, the fundamental working force which accelerates the apparatus is developed practically 
from zero. Thus, we can divide resistance exercises into two groups:
• Exercises in which the working force is developed after preliminary muscular tension (equal to the weight of
the apparatus)
• Exercises in which force is developed from zero, without appreciable preliminary muscular tension.
The main difference between these groups of exercises is that the exercises in the first group do not appreciably 
influence the processes connected with physiological changes in the muscles (the cxcitation-tension link). 
Consequently, depending upon the amount of weight used, conditions arc created chiefly for developing muscular 
strength or the speed of muscular contraction, but not the speed with which muscles switch from rest to the 
active state. The conditions of muscular work in the second group of exercises have the simultaneous potential 
for developing dynamic strength, speed of movement and especially starting strength. This is not simply relevant 
to understanding movement dynamics, but is very significant for improving strength training methods.
Finally, based upon the conditions under which force is applied, exercises should be distinguished by force 
directed against the weight o f a load and by force directed against the inertia o f a load. In the first case, if one lifts 
a barbell, for example, the working force of the movement is equal to F = m(g+a), i.e. determined by the mass of 
the load and the acceleration against gravity. In the second case, the force of the movement is equal to F = ma, i.e. 
dependent only upon the load’s force of inertia, moving with a certain acceleration. Examples o f such conditions 
arc throwing, sprinting out of the starting blocks and punching, i.e. those situations when strength operates in a 
direction approximately perpendicular to the gravitational force. The differences in the biomechanics of these 
types of movements are quite significant.
In the first case (overcoming weight), muscular force initially becomes equal to the amount of weight to be 
lifted (developed under virtually isometric conditions), then it exceeds it as motion begins, it proceeds to 
accelerate the load, and then it increases further as it exceeds the weight of the apparatus (sec Figs 2.1, 2.13). The 
preliminary isometric muscular tension causes a large gradient of acceleration-strength.
In the second case (overcoming inertia), if friction and the resistance of the surroundings are excluded, then 
movement of the load begins with insignificant propulsive force. Further changes in the latter are caused wholly 
by the speed of muscular contraction or, more precisely, the ability of the muscles to move the load by 
simultaneous production of maximal strength and maximum speed of contraction.
Consequently, under conditions where strength resists the weight of the load, primarily the strength 
component is stimulated. 
Under conditions where strength is directed against the 
inertia of the load, 
predominantly the speed of muscular contraction is stimulated.
218

######## IDX 230 (printed 219)
SUPERTRAINING
Thus, in the second case, it is easy to appreciate the possibility for overcoming the opposing tendency 
between the weight of the load and the speed of muscular contraction. Unfortunately, the necessary specialised 
quipment for producing muscular work to overcome the inertia of a load is rarely used in training. However, to 
extend the methods of special strength training, one must consider this concept of inertial training more seriously. 
There are two possible solutions: the application of force (e.g. a thrust) against a horizontal wheel or a suspended 
load (like a pendulum), or the spinning of a heavy flywheel ergometer by the arms or the legs (e.g. Fig 4.4). In 
the first example, one can vary the amount of weight and in the second, the moment of inertia of the flywheel to 
affect speed o f contraction. One may use upper body or lower body ergometer flywheel devices in several 
different ways - accelerating against high inertia, using the heavy wheel to compel one to operate at a certain 
cadence, and opposing the angular momentum via eccentric muscle action to decelerate the wheel. One may 
combine all of these methods in short bursts or mixed bursts to offer a varied training regime.
Work with weights should be examined as a special case. Weights are used extensively for increasing the 
difficulty of movement to develop various motor abilities. Elastic bands are also frequently used as a means of 
resisting movement, although the character o f the force produced depends upon the elastic properties of the 
material, which limits the effectiveness of these means. Elastic force occurs in accordance with Hooke's Law: F = 
Lx, where k is the spring constant and x is the extension. Thus, elastic force increases with degree of extension, so 
that resistance begins from zero value and increases with movement range. Therefore, elastic materials should not 
be used for developing starting-strength in ballistic movements or for developing explosive-strength.
Figure 4.4 Inertial Training by turning a flywheel via the use of elbow flexion (Vcrkhoshansky, 1977).
It is another matter regarding strength-endurance over a selected range. In this case, one can select the length and 
elasticity of the band so that its resistance will change minimally over the working amplitude of the movement. 
This method is sometimes used by swimmers for developing strength endurance in pulling movements (Fig 4.5).
Figure 4.5 Elasticised cable exercise for developing strength-endurance in swimming (Verkhoshansky, 1977).
In using elastics in general, the tension always increases with range of movement and this may readily be 
decreased at ‘sticking points* by moving towards the point of attachment of the bands, or conversely, if the 
tension is still not great enough, one can move away from the point of attachment. Thus, one can tend to 
overcome the major limitation of elastics, namely their nature to increase tension throughout the range (since 
tension is proportional to extension, according to Hooke’s Law). Resistance can be varied over the full range of 
movement by accelerating free weights when resistance is decreasing (so-called “Compensatory Acceleration 
Training’) or by using special varying resistance machines, and this method of altering elastic length by postural 
idjustment also allows one to use elastics to optimise resistance, if required.
The methods of resisted movement are extremely diverse. In each case they are determined by the exercise 
and the resolution of two tasks: stimulation of muscular contraction and facilitation of transfer to the natural 
conditions of the movement (for example, putting a regulation shot after training with an overweight one). 
Movements can be made more difficult with small weights, thereby insignificantly increasing the mass of the body 
or its links. This may be accomplished with belts, weights, cuffs, sandbags, boots and other apparatus.

726	overcoming significant resistance, then resistance exercises are definitely useful, but only in those eases when they

728	which is specific to the given sport.
729	4.2.3 K inetic Energy and Strength Processes
730	Consider the case where a training devicc, such as a barbell, possesses some velocity attained by falling from some 
731	height, and the athlete's task consists of first actively stopping it, then quickly thrusting it upwards (Fig 4.6).
732	Figure 4.6 Thrusting a load upwards after it has fallen from a given height. This plyometric bench press device was designed by R 
733	Adcock, A Chantler, H Glyn-Jones and T Rademeyer, students in the School of Mechanical Engineering at the University of the 
734	Witwatersrand as part of a senior biomechanics project (1992).
735	Under similar circumstances the total muscular working force developed by eccentric amortisation followed by 
736	active concentric work may be calculated from F = m(g+a), where the acceleration a = V2/2.s, from the equation
737	V2 = u2 + 2a.s:
738	F = m (V,2/2Sl + g) + m (V 22/2S2 + g).
739	where Vl, V2 refer to the velocity of the barbell at displacements Si and S 2 respectively, m is the mass of the 
740	barbell, and g is the acceleration due to gravity.
741	A characteristic of such a movement is that much of the kinetic energy of the apparatus is transformed during 
742	the amortisation phase into elastic energy, which is then used in the subsequent concentric work. If energy losses 
743	by processes such as heat generation and viscous damping in the muscle complcx are excluded as a first 
744	approximation, this elastic energy is equal to the kinetic energy of the apparatus at the end of its fall (ICE = mgh 
745	where m = mass, h = the height of the fall and g = acceleration due to gravity). The muscular force developed at 
746	the instant of switching from eccentric to concentric work will be greater for a shorter amortisation phase and a 
747	shorter braking time. This applies strictly to those conditions when the action as a whole is aimed at thrusting the 
748	apparatus with maximum speed immediately after it has been stopped.
749	220
750	
751	######## IDX 232 (printed 221)
752	SUPERTRAINING
753	Thus, what we are referring to is completely different from the traditional production of muscular tension. The 
754	external mechanical stimulus is not so much the weight (and its force of inertia) as the energy accumulated after its 
755	free-fall.
756	If one considers the dynamics of muscular work with variations of the take-off in the vertical jump for example 
757	(Fig 4.7), it may be seen that such a means of stimulating muscular tension offers significant advantages, namely:
758	1. It develops maximal dynamic force very rapidly
759	2. The magnitude of this maximum is significantly larger than that produced by other methods
760	3. A large maximal force is achieved without the use of additional resistance
761	4. Change from eccentric to concentric work occurs far more rapidly than with other methods
762	5. The significant elastic energy accumulated (without additional resistance) during the amortisation phase 
763	produces muscular work of greater power in the thrust phase and faster muscular contraction, which may 
764	be inferred from the greater height attained by the body during the subsequent upward drive.
765	Thus, stimulation of muscular tension by absorption of the energy of the athlete's falling body or a training 
766	apparatus can produce a large force of muscular contraction without using weights (which is impossible with 
767	other means of mechanical stimulation). This is achieved not only without decreasing the speed of muscular 
768	contraction, but even increasing it in comparison with the usual resistance methods.
769	Figure 4.7 The development of force for various vertical jumps: (1) jumping from rest from a low squat (2) the usual jump with a dip 
770	or amortisation phase (3) after a depth-jump from 0.4 metre. The jump heights reached were 0.67m, 0.74m and 0.80m respectively. 
771	(Verkhoshansky. 1977).
772	The first experimental steps taken to study this principle of muscular stimulation revealed its particular 
773	effectiveness in developing explosive strength and starting strength. The potential for developing starting strength 
774	generally is limited because it depends upon one's ability to concentrate intensively on a specific voluntary effort.
775	This strength is acquired very slowly in training because particularly stressful conditions are required, namely 
776	a stimulus of such intensity that it provokes the appropriate adaptive reaction. Even the wide variety of popular 
777	resistance strength exercises usually do not fulfill these requirements, despite the fact that they usually require 
778	force to be developed from rest.
779	Several studies suggest that such exercises can have a place if, for example, muscular tension is achieved by 
780	means of an abrupt stretch at the instant when a falling body or object is stopped (Ramsey, 1944; Hill, 1955; 
781	Tweit et al, 1963). It should be emphasized that significant and almost instantaneous development of muscular 
782	tension in this case is due to the mechanical stimulation of proprioceptors in the neuromuscular system, which 
783	creates the conditions for developing starting strength and explosiveness of muscular action.
784	Thus, we have a specific work regime which no heavy resistance exercise can imitate, because stimulation of 
785	muscular activity with significant extra resistance slows down the transition from eccentric to concentric work. 
786	The utilisation of energy of a falling body or object for mechanical stimulation requires the muscles to initially 
787	develop significant clastic tension, use it in overcoming the inertia of a relatively small weight then quickly switch 
788	to concentric work and produce a high speed of muscle contraction.
789	The role of kinetic energy in stimulating explosive muscle action warrants detailed analysis. To do this in the 
790	laboratory a special experimental stand was constructed to measure the height attained by a load when a subject 
791	threw it upward after it had first fallen from some height (from 0.5 to 3.0 metres). The kinetic energy used for
792	221
793	
794	######## IDX 233 (printed 222)
795	SUPERTRAINING
796	muscle stimulation changcd according to the weight (3.3, 6.6, 9.9 and 13.3% of the maximum isometric strength! | 
797	and the height of the fall (Vcrkhoshansky, 1977). The experiment showed that an increase in kinetic energy caused 
798	by an increase in the mass of the load decreases the height to which a load is thrown, but an increase in the 
799	distance through which a load falls increases the height to which it is thrown (Fig 4.8a).
800	A similar picture emerges from research on reactive ability (Fig 4.8b). This tendency, in general, is displayed 
801	by movements executed under other conditions, although these have their own peculiarities (Figs 4.9, 4.10). ] 
802	These examples show clearly that it is not beneficial to increase kinetic energy by use o f heavier loads. It is 
803	therefore necessary to examine a better means of increasing the thrust height. 
804	The depth jump which has 
805	immediate practical significance for developing jumping ability is given in the example illustrated in Figure 4.10. 
806	Here maximal force (Fmax) increases up to a height of 1.15 metres, then diminishes sharply, while movement time 
807	begins by changing insignificantly, then increasing sharply. Maximum power and reactivity are achieved using a 
808	drop height of approximately 0.75 metres.
809	Figure 4.8 (a) Changes in height (h2) o f thrown loads of different mass (in terms o f maximum isometric strength Po), after having 
810	fallen from different heights (hi) (b) Changes in reactivity coefficient (RC) with respect to the kinetic energy of the falling load. 
811	(Verkhoshansky, 1977).
812	Thus, the optimal range of depth jumping for the stimulation of muscular activity is 0.75-1.15 metres, because at 
813	the lower end of this range the muscles are working at maximal power and at the upper end they are working at 
814	maximal dynamic force. This finding forms the basis for the recommendations for using depth jumps in the 
815	training of advanced jumpers 
816	(Vcrkhoshansky 1963, 
817	1964, 1966), though it is preferable to err on the 
818	conservative side of using considerably lower jump heights with anyone who is unused to this type of training 
819	and to strictly limit the volume of this type o f ‘shock’ training.
820	Further increases in the height of the depth jump significantly decrease the magnitude of the dynamic 
821	parameters of the take-off. The support time increases quickly, primarily because the phase o f switching from 
822	eccentric to concentric work is lengthened. In addition, the maximum dynamic force of take-off and the speed of 
823	muscular contraction stabilise and do not increase any further.
824	The take-off comprises two distinct actions: amortisation (where the kinetic energy of the fall is absorbed), 
825	and the thrust proper. The amortisation is characterised by the increasing depth of the resulting knee flexion, and 
826	the thrust proper by a fairly constant speed of muscle contraction. 
827	Thus, the positive effect of muscle 
828	stimulation by absorption of kinetic energy from a fall can be used successfully only under certain conditions by 
829	taking into consideration the optimal height of the fall, bodymass, additional load, and any other factors which 
830	may facilitate a quick take-off.
831	However, the state of the neuromuscular system during the amortisation phase of the falling body also can 
832	play an independent training role. Tension developed reflexively during this phase enhances the ability of the 
833	muscles to switch quickly to the active state. Experience indicates that this is not detrimental to speed-strength
834	222
835	
836	######## IDX 234 (printed 223)
837	SUPERTRAINING
838	preparation and the musculoskeletal support apparatus, although further research is required in order to make 
839	definitive practical recommendations in this area.
840	Figure 4.10 Take-off characteristics after depth jumping from gradually greater heights (h). RC is the reactivity coefficient, Fmax is 
841	the maximal force and t is the ground contact time. (Vcrkhoshansky, 1977).
842	Therefore, muscle stimulation by the absorption of energy of a falling body can be a very effective method of 
843	loading, the basis of which lies in the ability of the muscles to contract more powerfully after a sharp preliminary 
844	stretch. This mechanism enables one to successfully overcome the force of body inertia in emergency situations, 
845	which proves to be of particular value in sport.
846	Preliminary muscle stretching has a place in a number of strength exercises such as squats and jumps with a 
847	barbell on the shoulders. However, these exercises are not as intensely impulsive as exercises which brake the 
848	velocity of a preliminary fall and display a sharp, shock-like character.
849	Therefore, the method of muscle stimulation by means of absorbing the kinetic energy of a fall, now known 
850	as plyometrics, was originally called the 'shock method' (Verkhoshansky 1966, 1968). 
851	Research by 
852	Vcrkhoshansky (1958, 1976) took the first serious steps in studying and formulating this method and much 
853	subsequent research has corroborated its effectiveness in specific applications (Kuznetsov, 1966; Papysheva, 
854	1966; Chudinov, 1966; Chemesheva, 1967; Semenov, 1967; Tatian, 1974; Khodykin, 1975). However, more 
855	work is needed in the laboratory and under training conditions before its full scope is covered.
856	4.2.4 Isom etric Training
857	In athletics, isometric exercises were very popular in the mid-1950s as a result of the search for economical and 
858	effective methods of developing strength. Hettinger and Muller (1953, 1955) established that one daily effort of 
859	two-thirds of one's maximum exerted for six seconds at a time for 10 weeks will increase strength about 5% per
860	223
861	
862	######## IDX 235 (printed 224)
863	SUPERTRAINING
864	week, while Clark et al (1954) found that static strength continues to increase even after the conclusion of a four- 
865	week programme of isomctric exercises.
866	The success of isometric training provoked considerable research, much of it being concerned with the 
867	question of its effectiveness compared with dynamic training. This research produced rather contradictory data 
868	(see review by Verkhoshansky, 1970). However, research produced the general conclusion that isometric training 
869	can be more effective than dynamic exercises in those cases where the specific exercise requires muscle contraction 
870	of large magnitude at a certain stage of a movement or during the early stages of injury rehabilitation.
871	If the specific exercise involves high-speed movement, then sustained isometric training is less effective. 
872	Research indicates that there are distinct differences between the training effects of static and dynamic exercises. 
873	It is important that muscular tension should be increased slowly and be held for a relatively long time when 
874	executing isometric exercises, because the usual purpose of isometric training is to develop absolute strength. 
875	Prolonged maintenance of muscular tension requires an energy expenditure which stimulates adequate adaptation 
876	in the neuromuscular system, thereby determining its strength potential. The increase in strength can be more 
877	significant than that produced by transient dynamic tension. If one notes the fact that some researchers have not 
878	discovered an essential difference in the growth of strength produced by muscle tension of various intensities, 
879	then it is obvious that the fundamental conditioning factor is not so much the magnitude of the isometric tension 
880	as its duration.
881	A technique which may be referred to as oscillatory isometrics may also be useful in producing powerful 
882	contractions over a small range of movement. This is corroborated by research which showed the maximum 
883	tension that can be produced voluntarily during sinusoidally pulsed brief isometric jerks at 5 Hz is the same as the 
884	maximum sustained tension (Soechting & Roberts, 1975). Basmajian (1978) commented that this emphasizes the 
885	importance of muscle fibre recruitment in the gradation of tension and synchronisation of motor unit activity 
886	during the short bursts of loading.
887	In other applications, short periods of low frequency mechanical vibration (10-35 Hz) on the body have been 
888	shown to induce faster recovery, have a positive effect on different body systems, modulate muscle activity, elicit 
889	a higher stable state of strength and power, lower arterial pressure, and enhance oxidative processes (Kopysov, 
890	1978; Lebedev & Peliakov, 1991). More recently, it has been found that powerful whole body vibrations 
891	imposed at 26 Hz through the lower extremities produces marked increases in jumping power (Bosco et al, 1998).
892	These findings may relate to a similar impulsive loading process which is associated with the training effects 
893	of plyometrics, thereby adding further fuel to the debate (Ingen Schcnau ct al, 1997) about which of the following 
894	effects may predominate during plyometrics: elastic energy storage/utilisation in the soft tissues, neural 
895	facilitation or intrinsic muscle changes.
896	At this point it must be stressed that isometric training is not simply a matter o f holding a static muscle 
897	contraction for a given time. Isometric contraction requires a muscle to increase its tension from rest to a 
898	maximum or sub-maximal value over a certain time (rise or ‘attack’ time), to sustain this tension for another period 
899	(the resistance phase) and to decrease this tension to rest or a lower value (decay time). Consequently, one may 
900	distinguish between explosive isometrics, which have a very brief rise time, and slow isometrics, with a much 
901	longer rise time (Fig 4.12). The isometric contraction may be produced by voluntary contraction or involuntarily 
902	by the reflex response of the muscle between the eccentric and concentric phases of plyometric activities such as 
903	the depth jump or weightlifting clean-and-jerk. The different types of isometric contraction are categorised in 
904	Figure 4.11.
905	Each class of isometric training produces its own distinct training effects. If isometric exercises are executed 
906	with the accent on the speed of developing force, then they can be as effective for developing explosive strength 
907	as dynamic exercises. The steepness of the force-time curve (Fig 3.3) and the greater magnitude of maximum 
908	isometric than dynamic maximum force for equivalent joint angles is the basis for this assertion. Therefore, it is 
909	doubtful whether it is always productive to maintain a rigid distinction between dynamic and isometric exercise. In 
910	general, the harder the muscles work in overcoming large resistance, the more closcly the work becomes isometric, 
911	as may be seen from the force-vclocity curves of muscle action (Figs 3.15 & 3.16). In other words, isometric 
912	work is really the limiting case o f dynamic work as the velocity o f movement tends to zero. Furthermore, because 
913	the inhibitory effects usually associated with voluntary muscle action are not encountered in reflexive isometric 
914	contraction, even greater explosive force can be displayed isometrically than dynamically.
915	224
916

threw it upward after it had first fallen from some height (from 0.5 to 3.0 metres). The kinetic energy used for
221

######## IDX 233 (printed 222)
SUPERTRAINING
muscle stimulation changcd according to the weight (3.3, 6.6, 9.9 and 13.3% of the maximum isometric strength! | 
and the height of the fall (Vcrkhoshansky, 1977). The experiment showed that an increase in kinetic energy caused 
by an increase in the mass of the load decreases the height to which a load is thrown, but an increase in the 
distance through which a load falls increases the height to which it is thrown (Fig 4.8a).
A similar picture emerges from research on reactive ability (Fig 4.8b). This tendency, in general, is displayed 
by movements executed under other conditions, although these have their own peculiarities (Figs 4.9, 4.10). ] 
These examples show clearly that it is not beneficial to increase kinetic energy by use o f heavier loads. It is 
therefore necessary to examine a better means of increasing the thrust height. 
The depth jump which has 
immediate practical significance for developing jumping ability is given in the example illustrated in Figure 4.10. 
Here maximal force (Fmax) increases up to a height of 1.15 metres, then diminishes sharply, while movement time 
begins by changing insignificantly, then increasing sharply. Maximum power and reactivity are achieved using a 
drop height of approximately 0.75 metres.
Figure 4.8 (a) Changes in height (h2) o f thrown loads of different mass (in terms o f maximum isometric strength Po), after having 
fallen from different heights (hi) (b) Changes in reactivity coefficient (RC) with respect to the kinetic energy of the falling load. 
(Verkhoshansky, 1977).
Thus, the optimal range of depth jumping for the stimulation of muscular activity is 0.75-1.15 metres, because at 
the lower end of this range the muscles are working at maximal power and at the upper end they are working at 
maximal dynamic force. This finding forms the basis for the recommendations for using depth jumps in the 
training of advanced jumpers 
(Vcrkhoshansky 1963, 
1964, 1966), though it is preferable to err on the 
conservative side of using considerably lower jump heights with anyone who is unused to this type of training 
and to strictly limit the volume of this type o f ‘shock’ training.
Further increases in the height of the depth jump significantly decrease the magnitude of the dynamic 
parameters of the take-off. The support time increases quickly, primarily because the phase o f switching from 
eccentric to concentric work is lengthened. In addition, the maximum dynamic force of take-off and the speed of 
muscular contraction stabilise and do not increase any further.
The take-off comprises two distinct actions: amortisation (where the kinetic energy of the fall is absorbed), 
and the thrust proper. The amortisation is characterised by the increasing depth of the resulting knee flexion, and 
the thrust proper by a fairly constant speed of muscle contraction. 
Thus, the positive effect of muscle 
stimulation by absorption of kinetic energy from a fall can be used successfully only under certain conditions by 
taking into consideration the optimal height of the fall, bodymass, additional load, and any other factors which 
may facilitate a quick take-off.
However, the state of the neuromuscular system during the amortisation phase of the falling body also can 
play an independent training role. Tension developed reflexively during this phase enhances the ability of the 
muscles to switch quickly to the active state. Experience indicates that this is not detrimental to speed-strength
222

######## IDX 234 (printed 223)
SUPERTRAINING
preparation and the musculoskeletal support apparatus, although further research is required in order to make 
definitive practical recommendations in this area.
Figure 4.10 Take-off characteristics after depth jumping from gradually greater heights (h). RC is the reactivity coefficient, Fmax is 
the maximal force and t is the ground contact time. (Vcrkhoshansky, 1977).
Therefore, muscle stimulation by the absorption of energy of a falling body can be a very effective method of 
loading, the basis of which lies in the ability of the muscles to contract more powerfully after a sharp preliminary 
stretch. This mechanism enables one to successfully overcome the force of body inertia in emergency situations, 
which proves to be of particular value in sport.
Preliminary muscle stretching has a place in a number of strength exercises such as squats and jumps with a 
barbell on the shoulders. However, these exercises are not as intensely impulsive as exercises which brake the 
velocity of a preliminary fall and display a sharp, shock-like character.
Therefore, the method of muscle stimulation by means of absorbing the kinetic energy of a fall, now known 
as plyometrics, was originally called the 'shock method' (Verkhoshansky 1966, 1968). 
Research by 
Vcrkhoshansky (1958, 1976) took the first serious steps in studying and formulating this method and much 
subsequent research has corroborated its effectiveness in specific applications (Kuznetsov, 1966; Papysheva, 
1966; Chudinov, 1966; Chemesheva, 1967; Semenov, 1967; Tatian, 1974; Khodykin, 1975). However, more 
work is needed in the laboratory and under training conditions before its full scope is covered.
4.2.4 Isom etric Training
In athletics, isometric exercises were very popular in the mid-1950s as a result of the search for economical and 
effective methods of developing strength. Hettinger and Muller (1953, 1955) established that one daily effort of 
two-thirds of one's maximum exerted for six seconds at a time for 10 weeks will increase strength about 5% per
223

######## IDX 235 (printed 224)
SUPERTRAINING
week, while Clark et al (1954) found that static strength continues to increase even after the conclusion of a four- 
week programme of isomctric exercises.
The success of isometric training provoked considerable research, much of it being concerned with the 
question of its effectiveness compared with dynamic training. This research produced rather contradictory data 
(see review by Verkhoshansky, 1970). However, research produced the general conclusion that isometric training 
can be more effective than dynamic exercises in those cases where the specific exercise requires muscle contraction 
of large magnitude at a certain stage of a movement or during the early stages of injury rehabilitation.
If the specific exercise involves high-speed movement, then sustained isometric training is less effective. 
Research indicates that there are distinct differences between the training effects of static and dynamic exercises. 
It is important that muscular tension should be increased slowly and be held for a relatively long time when 
executing isometric exercises, because the usual purpose of isometric training is to develop absolute strength. 
Prolonged maintenance of muscular tension requires an energy expenditure which stimulates adequate adaptation 
in the neuromuscular system, thereby determining its strength potential. The increase in strength can be more 
significant than that produced by transient dynamic tension. If one notes the fact that some researchers have not 
discovered an essential difference in the growth of strength produced by muscle tension of various intensities, 
then it is obvious that the fundamental conditioning factor is not so much the magnitude of the isometric tension 
as its duration.
A technique which may be referred to as oscillatory isometrics may also be useful in producing powerful 
contractions over a small range of movement. This is corroborated by research which showed the maximum 
tension that can be produced voluntarily during sinusoidally pulsed brief isometric jerks at 5 Hz is the same as the 
maximum sustained tension (Soechting & Roberts, 1975). Basmajian (1978) commented that this emphasizes the 
importance of muscle fibre recruitment in the gradation of tension and synchronisation of motor unit activity 
during the short bursts of loading.
In other applications, short periods of low frequency mechanical vibration (10-35 Hz) on the body have been 
shown to induce faster recovery, have a positive effect on different body systems, modulate muscle activity, elicit 
a higher stable state of strength and power, lower arterial pressure, and enhance oxidative processes (Kopysov, 
1978; Lebedev & Peliakov, 1991). More recently, it has been found that powerful whole body vibrations 
imposed at 26 Hz through the lower extremities produces marked increases in jumping power (Bosco et al, 1998).
These findings may relate to a similar impulsive loading process which is associated with the training effects 
of plyometrics, thereby adding further fuel to the debate (Ingen Schcnau ct al, 1997) about which of the following 
effects may predominate during plyometrics: elastic energy storage/utilisation in the soft tissues, neural 
facilitation or intrinsic muscle changes.
At this point it must be stressed that isometric training is not simply a matter o f holding a static muscle 
contraction for a given time. Isometric contraction requires a muscle to increase its tension from rest to a 
maximum or sub-maximal value over a certain time (rise or ‘attack’ time), to sustain this tension for another period 
(the resistance phase) and to decrease this tension to rest or a lower value (decay time). Consequently, one may 
distinguish between explosive isometrics, which have a very brief rise time, and slow isometrics, with a much 
longer rise time (Fig 4.12). The isometric contraction may be produced by voluntary contraction or involuntarily 
by the reflex response of the muscle between the eccentric and concentric phases of plyometric activities such as 
the depth jump or weightlifting clean-and-jerk. The different types of isometric contraction are categorised in 
Figure 4.11.
Each class of isometric training produces its own distinct training effects. If isometric exercises are executed 
with the accent on the speed of developing force, then they can be as effective for developing explosive strength 
as dynamic exercises. The steepness of the force-time curve (Fig 3.3) and the greater magnitude of maximum 
isometric than dynamic maximum force for equivalent joint angles is the basis for this assertion. Therefore, it is 
doubtful whether it is always productive to maintain a rigid distinction between dynamic and isometric exercise. In 
general, the harder the muscles work in overcoming large resistance, the more closcly the work becomes isometric, 
as may be seen from the force-vclocity curves of muscle action (Figs 3.15 & 3.16). In other words, isometric 
work is really the limiting case o f dynamic work as the velocity o f movement tends to zero. Furthermore, because 
the inhibitory effects usually associated with voluntary muscle action are not encountered in reflexive isometric 
contraction, even greater explosive force can be displayed isometrically than dynamically.

    13	
    14	# The Authors' MACS/MICS Theory of Electrostimulation: Macro-Current as Stressor, Micro-Current as Non-Stressor
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors state that "electric currents as much as 1000 times smaller
    17	than that of all the traditional physical therapy modalities can be far more successful than
    18	the latter in achieving many of the benefits outlined in the previous section", and that
    19	currents as low as 10 microamps pulsating at 0.1 to 400 Hz, too weak to cause contraction,
    20	block pain signals or cause local heating, have an "effectiveness and safety [that] is often
    21	superior in many applications to that of faradism, interferentialism and conventional TENS"
    22	(Matteson & Eberhardt, 1985) (PDF p. 224, printed p. 213). From this they propose an
    23	integrated theory, introduced with "it appears as if": macroelectric cellular stimulation
    24	(**MACS**, currents exceeding one milliamp) acts as a physiological stressor producing the
    25	alarm response described by Selye (1975). They cite Eriksson et al (1981), who found the
    26	acute effects of traditional ES similar to those of intense voluntary exercise, and Gambke et
    27	al (1985), who found in animal studies that long-term MACS causes some muscle fibres, mainly
    28	FT fibres, to degenerate a few days after ES and be replaced by new fibres from
    29	satellite-cell proliferation. Applying Selye's model (see 1.16), the body would draw on its
    30	superficial adaptation energy stores to adapt to MACS by increasing strength or endurance, or
    31	by fibre-type transformation; if the ES is too intense, too prolonged or inappropriately
    32	used, adaptation might not occur or might increase the proportion of slow-twitch fibres and
    33	reduce strength, and "excessively demanding MACS conceivably might cause the body to draw on
    34	its deep adaptation energy and lead to permanent tissue damage" (PDF p. 225, printed p. 214).
    35	Microelectric cellular stimulation (**MICS**, currents below one milliamp) "would not act as
    36	a stressor"; it is said to elicit biochemical changes tied to "resonant attunement of the
    37	stimulus to cellular and subcellular processes" (p.214). The supporting findings cited: Becker
    38	and colleagues on sub-threshold modulation of electric fields across nerve and glial cells,
    39	including accelerated wound healing and partial limb regeneration in amphibians and rats
    40	(Becker, 1974; Becker & Marino, 1982); Nordenstrom's "closed electric circuits" carrying ionic
    41	flow along blood vessels (Nordenstrom, 1983); Pilla's (1974) membrane-signalling model and
    42	cellular "windows" that open most effectively to certain frequencies, pulse widths and
    43	amplitudes (Pilla, 1981); Rodan et al (1978), who found 5 Hz ES stimulated DNA synthesis in
    44	chick cartilage cells and rat bone by as much as 27% (but not in chick skin fibroblasts or rat
    45	spleen lymphocytes) 4-6 hours after 15 minutes of ES; and Cheng et al (1982), who found
    46	50-1000 microamp currents increased rat tissue ATP by 300-500% and amino-acid transport and
    47	protein synthesis by as much as 40%, while currents above one milliamp depressed ATP and
    48	protein synthesis (traditional ES usually exceeds 20 milliamps, at which the depression is
    49	"nearly 50%") (PDF p. 224, printed p. 213).
    50	
    51	Safety statements attached to the theory. The authors state "It is generally entirely safe
    52	to apply MICS anywhere on the body" (p.214) and that MICS "cannot produce overtraining or
    53	injury" (PDF p. 226, printed p. 215). They give no safety data; the claim follows from their
    54	MICS model. They also state that "Under no circumstances should MACS be applied across the
    55	brain, as it can cause serious harm", and that "It is generally not advisable to apply any
    56	form of ES to epileptics, pregnant women, cardiac patients or persons with heart pacemakers"
    57	(PDF p. 225, printed p. 214). A counterweight in the same section: "routine or frequent use
    58	of accelerated methods of restoration can impair the natural ability of the body to
    59	recuperate and adapt; it is sometimes important to allow the body to undergo partial or
    60	unaccelerated restoration to facilitate the supercompensatory response (Siff & Yessis,
    61	1992)" (PDF p. 227, printed p. 216). (PDF pp. 224-227, printed pp. 213-216, "4.2.1.4 Further
    62	Research Findings", "4.2.1.5 An Integrated Theory of Electrostimulation" and "4.2.1.6 The Use
    63	of Electrostimulation in Training.")
    64	
    65	**Why it works** — This is the authors' own proposed synthesis. Inference: it rests on two
    66	threads of different standing: (a) the point that MACS-range ES acts as a training stressor
    67	subject to dose-response and overtraining risk (the Selye, Eriksson and Gambke citations);
    68	and (b) a set of bioelectric claims (Becker's regeneration work, Nordenstrom's closed
    69	circuits, Pilla's cellular windows) offered as a general theory of cell communication.
    70	Inference: thread (b) has not, as far as this ingest has checked, entered mainstream
    71	sports-science or clinical practice; no named source for that judgment is given here. The
    72	authors use the limits of the action-potential model as an argument for their alternative:
    73	"little is known about electrical fields at the subcellular level", and classical theory
    74	does not explain "the repair of fractures, the healing of wounds and reduction of
    75	thrombosis" (PDF p. 221, printed p. 210).
    76	
    77	**When to apply** — Inference: the (a) thread, that macro-current ES functions as a stressor
    78	requiring progressive dosing rather than a fixed protocol, is consistent with basic
    79	training-load principles and does not depend on accepting thread (b). The authors' own
    80	dosing statement: an athlete who benefits from MACS "should not assume that increased dosage
    81	will lead to further improvement. The contrary may well prove to be true" (p.214). Inference:
    82	do not use this entry to justify low-current "microcurrent" devices for performance or
    83	healing claims without independent, modern verification outside this book.
    84	
    85	**When NOT to apply** — Marked `contested`. Inference: several supporting claims in thread
    86	(b) (glial cells acting like semiconductors, Nordenstrom's closed circuits, "resonant
    87	attunement" as the operative principle of MICS) are not treated here as independently
    88	replicated physiology, and this entry does not verify them against current literature. The
    89	Rodan (1978) and Cheng (1982) findings are animal and cell studies (chick cartilage, rat bone,
    90	rat tissue) at narrow current ranges; they do not establish that MICS produces general
    91	"adaptation, growth and repair" effects in human athletes. The MICS safety claims (p.214,
    92	p.215) come without safety data. Inference: "MACS" and "MICS" appear to be the authors' own
    93	terms for this section.
    94	
    95	**Example** — Inference: a practitioner who reads that 10-microamp devices are more effective
    96	and safer than faradic stimulators should recognise that the claim is the authors' (citing
    97	Matteson & Eberhardt, 1985, p.213) and that its explanation rests on thread (b) (Becker,
    98	Nordenstrom, Pilla), and should keep the authors' own contraindications (p.214) in force
    99	whatever the device.
   100	
   101	**Related** — [[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]],
   102	[[heuristic--nine-reasons-electrostimulation-research-conflicts]] (item 9, the alternative
   103	physiological models),
   104	[[heuristic--electrostimulation-sequencing-dosage-and-safety-practicalities]] (the practical
   105	dosing limits and safety rules).

    14	# Ratov's Functional Electrostimulation (FES): Timing the Current to the Athlete's Own EMG Signal During the Sport Skill Itself
    15	
    16	**What it is** — In the 4.2.1 introduction the authors state that Ratov "has found that
    17	functional electrical stimulation (FENS) can be particularly useful in improving sporting
    18	performance". His techniques, developed from his PhD programme on the interrelation between
    19	electrical stimulation and electromyography, use EMG signals from agonist and antagonist
    20	muscles "to act as triggers or control mechanisms for electrical stimulation of muscles
    21	directly involved in producing functional movements in sport". In his laboratory at the State
    22	Central Institute for Sports Science in Moscow "he has successfully implemented these
    23	neuromuscular stimulation methods in training athletes such as fencers, boxers, rowers,
    24	shotputters and weightlifters" (PDF p. 219, printed p. 208).
    25	
    26	In 4.2.1.6 the authors note that "little or no mention is made in the West of the
    27	application of FES (Functional Electrostimulation) in sports training". In the West, FES or
    28	its equivalent FENS (Functional Electroneural Stimulation) refers to ES that contracts the
    29	muscles of spinally disabled patients who cannot voluntarily activate them. In Russia and
    30	other Eastern European countries the terms can also mean applying ES to able-bodied athletes
    31	during natural sporting movements "to intensify muscle tension at the most appropriate phases
    32	of these movements". Professor Igor Ratov "stresses that this type of functional stimulation
    33	is far more consistently successful than the passive methods attributed to Kots by his
    34	Western supporters" (see [[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]]).
    35	Siff writes in the first person: "Work that I witnessed in his laboratory involved the use of
    36	concurrent EMG recordings to phase the FES correctly into specific sporting movements, most
    37	specifically to avoid producing spurious muscle tension or uncoordinated movement."
    38	Eventually athletes learn to contract synchronously with the applied field "and thereby
    39	produce greater strength, power and speed". This is sometimes called active
    40	electrostimulation (ES applied to active muscles), as distinct from passive
    41	electrostimulation (applied to relaxed muscles), the method most common in physical therapy
    42	(PDF p. 226, printed p. 215). (PDF p. 219, printed p. 208, "4.2.1 Electrostimulation"; PDF
    43	p. 226, printed p. 215, "Sports Functional Electrostimulation.")
    44	
    45	**Why it works** — The stated logic: because the stimulus is phased by concurrent EMG into
    46	the correct part of the movement, it avoids "spurious muscle tension or uncoordinated
    47	movement" (p.215). Inference: no data (strength-gain percentages, EMG changes, performance
    48	results) are reported for this method in these passages; the claim of superiority over
    49	passive ES is Ratov's stated position as reported by the authors, not a cited experimental
    50	comparison.
    51	
    52	**When to apply** — Inference: relevant to anyone considering EMG-triggered or
    53	movement-phased electrical stimulation for sport-specific training (as opposed to general or
    54	isolated-muscle ES); the distinguishing feature to look for in any modern device or protocol
    55	claiming this lineage is EMG-based triggering synchronised to the athlete's own movement,
    56	not a fixed timing schedule.
    57	
    58	**When NOT to apply** — Untested: no quantitative outcome data are reported for Ratov's
    59	method in these passages, only a description of the approach, the authors' statement that he
    60	"successfully implemented" it with named sport groups (p.208), and Siff's first-hand
    61	observation (p.215). The claimed superiority over passive ES ("far more consistently
    62	successful") is Ratov's own assessment as reported, not verified against a cited trial.
    63	Inference: access to this method also depended on specialised laboratory equipment
    64	(EMG-linked stimulators) not generally available. Inference: the only numbers from Ratov's
    65	group in this section are Ratov & Kryazhev (1986), ES during cycling and speed skating (see
    66	[[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]], item 16, p.213).
    67	Whether that work used EMG-triggered FES is not stated.
    68	
    69	**Example** — The book's own example is Ratov's application with fencers, boxers, rowers,
    70	shotputters and weightlifters (p.208), with the EMG phasing Siff witnessed (p.215); no
    71	further example is added here.
    72	
    73	**Related** — [[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]],
    74	[[case-study--reding-electrostimulation-protocol-siff-account]],
    75	[[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]] (item 16, Ratov &
    76	Kryazhev 1986).

    13	
    14	# Practical Rules for Integrating Electrostimulation Into a Programme: Sequencing, Electrode Placement, Dose Limits
    15	
    16	**What it is** — "Several researchers (Purvin, Deniskin, Khodykin)", cited without dates,
    17	studied how electrostimulation (ES) combines with other training means. They found that ES
    18	first, followed by plyometrics, produces a greater training effect than the reverse order;
    19	"a still larger effect was obtained by using ES and plyometrics concurrently with heavy
    20	resistance exercise", while the ES and plyometric combination had its smallest training
    21	effect during periods of complete or partial rest (PDF pp. 225-226, printed pp. 214-215).
    22	Electrode placement matters: adjacent (close) attachment localises the contraction and keeps
    23	it fairly superficial, while distant attachment (one electrode at a remote or fairly neutral
    24	site) produces a more extensive, deeper contraction; electrode gel or weak saline solution is
    25	needed for comfortable conduction, and skin irritation or prickliness "invariably" results
    26	from the gel drying out. Electrodes may be placed directly over important nerves, but "the
    27	intensity of the ensuing contraction can be harmful" and this method "should be restricted to
    28	use by experienced physical therapists" (PDF p. 226, printed p. 215). On dosing: it is
    29	"generally not advisable to apply more than 5-10 minutes of intense ES per major muscle
    30	group, due to the associated tissue necrosis and prolonged soreness that may follow in the
    31	days after treatment"; biofeedback TENS devices that monitor cellular electrical
    32	characteristics and adjust parameters automatically limit the possibility of overstimulation
    33	or cell damage (p.215). An athlete who benefits from MACS (macro-current ES) "should not
    34	assume that increased dosage will lead to further improvement. The contrary may well prove
    35	to be true" (PDF p. 225, printed p. 214; see
    36	[[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]]).
    37	
    38	Safety rules, stated by the authors (PDF p. 225, printed p. 214): "Under no circumstances
    39	should MACS be applied across the brain, as it can cause serious harm." "It is generally not
    40	advisable to apply any form of ES to epileptics, pregnant women, cardiac patients or persons
    41	with heart pacemakers." They also state that it is "generally entirely safe to apply MICS
    42	anywhere on the body" (p.214), a claim for which they give no safety data (see the MACS/MICS
    43	entry).
    44	
    45	The authors' closing recommendation is that "the untutored reader is not encouraged to use
    46	ES, since it requires considerable theoretical and practical training for its safe and
    47	effective application"; casual users generally note sporadic or short-term progress and stop
    48	after a few months. "In several countries (such as the USA), ES devices generally may not be
    49	sold to the public or used commercially or therapeutically on any clients by anyone who is
    50	not trained in medicine or physiotherapy" (PDF p. 227, printed p. 216). Inference: this is
    51	the authors' statement at the time of writing; current regulation is not checked here.
    52	(PDF pp. 225-227, printed pp. 214-216, "4.2.1.5" and "4.2.1.6 The Use of Electrostimulation
    53	in Training.")
    54	
    55	**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for the sequencing or placement findings.
    56	For the dose limit they cite tissue necrosis and prolonged soreness (p.215). Inference:
    57	potentiation from ES before plyometrics, and current path between electrodes, are plausible
    58	but not stated. Inference: the sequencing result can be read as an instance of the book's
    59	training-order argument (see [[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]]).
    60	
    61	**When to apply** — Use the sequencing finding (ES before plyometrics gave a larger effect
    62	than plyometrics before ES; ES and plyometrics concurrent with heavy resistance gave a larger
    63	effect than ES followed by plyometrics) as a specific instance of the book's
    64	non-commutative training-order argument when programming ES within a session. Use the 5-10
    65	minute per-muscle-group ceiling and the electrode-placement guidance as baseline limits if
    66	ES is added to a programme, restrict direct-over-nerve placement to experienced physical
    67	therapists, and apply the p.214 contraindications without exception.
    68	
    69	**When NOT to apply** — The sequencing citations (Purvin, Deniskin, Khodykin) give no dates,
    70	sample sizes or effect sizes in this passage, only a directional ranking of conditions.
    71	Inference: treat it as a single-lab directional finding, not a quantified prescription. The
    72	authors' recommendation against untutored use, and the legal restrictions they cite, mean
    73	this entry is not a self-administration guide. Inference: for ES used as recovery, the
    74	Dupuy et al 2018 meta-analysis found that electrostimulation did not significantly improve
    75	DOMS or fatigue in the pooled analyses (vault entry, p.11):
    76	[[research-papers/dupuy-2018-an-evidence-based-approach-for-choosing-post-exercise-recovery-techniques-to-reduce-marker]]
    77	
    78	**Example** — Inference: a strength coach considering ES in a plyometric-heavy block would,

    14	# Muscle Recruitment Stays Fairly Consistent at Moderate Loads but Shifts Toward Proximal Muscles as Resistance or Velocity Rises
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Two related findings on how muscle involvement changes with load and
    17	velocity during repetitive barbell lifting. First, the "most stable indicator" of
    18	coordinated muscular activity in repetitive lifting is the sequential involvement of the
    19	same specific muscles across reps: in an experiment at 60% of 1RM, the muscles taking part
    20	in the work remained the same for 82% of the time "in all athletes"; at 80% of 1RM,
    21	consistency was lower (showing greater individuality), but "was higher for qualified
    22	athletes", and fatigue also disrupted coordination (Pakhomov, 1967). The
    23	relative contribution of participating muscles can also change during repetitive work
    24	(Lazareva, 1966; Kozlov, 1966), and the number of muscle groups involved can either decrease
    25	(Moikin, 1964) or increase (Averyanov, 1963). Second, movements executed
    26	with little effort or low velocity involve mostly the muscles of the body's distal links
    27	(Tochilov, 1946; Kosilov, 1948; Vinogradov, 1951); against significant resistance or at high
    28	velocity, activity characteristically shifts to the muscles of the proximal links, "which
    29	tend to play a more tonic or postural role." The authors draw a direct implication from this
    30	second finding: "muscle isolation under conditions of significant resistance is impossible,"
    31	a point developed later in the chapter (see
    32	[[claim--muscle-isolation-is-load-dependent-mostly-illusory-under-heavy-load]]). (PDF p.
    33	229, printed p. 218, "4.2.2 Resistance and Strength Training.")

    36	1RM (82%) exceeds that at 80% of 1RM, only the observation that consistency at the higher
    37	load "was higher for qualified athletes", and that fatigue disrupts
    38	it further. Inference: this is consistent with the general principle that skilled athletes
    39	have more stable, better-rehearsed motor patterns, which higher loads and fatigue both stress
    40	more than lower loads. For the proximal/distal shift, the authors give no mechanism beyond
    41	the empirical citations; Inference: this is plausibly related to proximal muscles' larger
    42	cross-sectional area and postural/stabilising role becoming more necessary as the system
    43	must resist larger external forces or move faster.
    44

    46	a caution when interpreting EMG or force-plate data collected across a set: which muscles are
    47	active can itself change with load and fatigue, independent of the athlete's technique
    48	intent. Inference: use the proximal/distal shift finding when auditing exercise selection
    49	for "isolation" claims at high resistance, and expect proximal, postural muscle involvement
    50	to increase, not stay constant, as load or velocity rises. Eric's baseline: "Metric
    51	selection for force-plate reporting follows a disciplined framework: pick 1-2 output metrics
    52	..., 1-3 driver metrics ..., 1-3 strategy metrics (how the athlete achieved it, e.g. phase
    53	durations)" (method-baseline.md, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring", tagged "Adopted

    55	may shift with load for the reasons in this claim.

    58	Lazareva/Kozlov 1966; Moikin 1964; Averyanov 1963; Tochilov 1946; Kosilov 1948; Vinogradov
    59	1951) without reported sample sizes, exercise types, or modern replication in this text; the

    14	# The Authors' MACS/MICS Theory of Electrostimulation: Macro-Current as Stressor, Micro-Current as Non-Stressor
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors state that "electric currents as much as 1000 times smaller
    17	than that of all the traditional physical therapy modalities can be far more successful than
    18	the latter in achieving many of the benefits outlined in the previous section", and that
    19	currents as low as 10 microamps pulsating at 0.1 to 400 Hz, too weak to cause contraction,
    20	block pain signals or cause local heating, have an "effectiveness and safety [that] is often
    21	superior in many applications to that of faradism, interferentialism and conventional TENS"
    22	(Matteson & Eberhardt, 1985) (PDF p. 224, printed p. 213). From this they propose an
    23	integrated theory, introduced with "it appears as if": macroelectric cellular stimulation
    24	(**MACS**, currents exceeding one milliamp) acts as a physiological stressor producing the
    25	alarm response described by Selye (1975). They cite Eriksson et al (1981), who found the
    26	acute effects of traditional ES similar to those of intense voluntary exercise, and Gambke et
    27	al (1985), who found in animal studies that long-term MACS causes some muscle fibres, mainly
    28	FT fibres, to degenerate a few days after ES and be replaced by new fibres from
    29	satellite-cell proliferation. Applying Selye's model (see 1.16), the body would draw on its
    30	superficial adaptation energy stores to adapt to MACS by increasing strength or endurance, or
    31	by fibre-type transformation; if the ES is too intense, too prolonged or inappropriately
    32	used, adaptation might not occur or might increase the proportion of slow-twitch fibres and
    33	reduce strength, and "excessively demanding MACS conceivably might cause the body to draw on
    34	its deep adaptation energy and lead to permanent tissue damage" (PDF p. 225, printed p. 214).
    35	Microelectric cellular stimulation (**MICS**, currents below one milliamp) "would not act as
    36	a stressor"; it is said to elicit biochemical changes tied to "resonant attunement of the
    37	stimulus to cellular and subcellular processes" (p.214). The supporting findings cited: Becker
    38	and colleagues on sub-threshold modulation of electric fields across nerve and glial cells,
    39	including accelerated wound healing and partial limb regeneration in amphibians and rats
    40	(Becker, 1974; Becker & Marino, 1982); Nordenstrom's "closed electric circuits" carrying ionic
    41	flow along blood vessels (Nordenstrom, 1983); Pilla's (1974) membrane-signalling model and
    42	cellular "windows" that open most effectively to certain frequencies, pulse widths and
    43	amplitudes (Pilla, 1981); Rodan et al (1978), who found 5 Hz ES stimulated DNA synthesis in
    44	chick cartilage cells and rat bone by as much as 27% (but not in chick skin fibroblasts or rat
    45	spleen lymphocytes) 4-6 hours after 15 minutes of ES; and Cheng et al (1982), who found
    46	50-1000 microamp currents increased rat tissue ATP by 300-500% and amino-acid transport and
    47	protein synthesis by as much as 40%, while currents above one milliamp depressed ATP and
    48	protein synthesis (traditional ES usually exceeds 20 milliamps, at which the depression is
    49	"nearly 50%") (PDF p. 224, printed p. 213).
    50	
    51	Safety statements attached to the theory. The authors state "It is generally entirely safe
    52	to apply MICS anywhere on the body" (p.214) and that MICS "cannot produce overtraining or
    53	injury" (PDF p. 226, printed p. 215). They give no safety data; the claim follows from their
    54	MICS model. They also state that "Under no circumstances should MACS be applied across the
    55	brain, as it can cause serious harm", and that "It is generally not advisable to apply any
    56	form of ES to epileptics, pregnant women, cardiac patients or persons with heart pacemakers"
    57	(PDF p. 225, printed p. 214). A counterweight in the same section: "routine or frequent use
    58	of accelerated methods of restoration can impair the natural ability of the body to
    59	recuperate and adapt; it is sometimes important to allow the body to undergo partial or
    60	unaccelerated restoration to facilitate the supercompensatory response (Siff & Yessis,
    61	1992)" (PDF p. 227, printed p. 216). (PDF pp. 224-227, printed pp. 213-216, "4.2.1.4 Further
    62	Research Findings", "4.2.1.5 An Integrated Theory of Electrostimulation" and "4.2.1.6 The Use
    63	of Electrostimulation in Training.")
    64	
    65	**Why it works** — This is the authors' own proposed synthesis. Inference: it rests on two
    66	threads of different standing: (a) the point that MACS-range ES acts as a training stressor
    67	subject to dose-response and overtraining risk (the Selye, Eriksson and Gambke citations);
    68	and (b) a set of bioelectric claims (Becker's regeneration work, Nordenstrom's closed
    69	circuits, Pilla's cellular windows) offered as a general theory of cell communication.
    70	Inference: thread (b) has not, as far as this ingest has checked, entered mainstream
    71	sports-science or clinical practice; no named source for that judgment is given here. The
    72	authors use the limits of the action-potential model as an argument for their alternative:
    73	"little is known about electrical fields at the subcellular level", and classical theory
    74	does not explain "the repair of fractures, the healing of wounds and reduction of
    75	thrombosis" (PDF p. 221, printed p. 210).

    78	requiring progressive dosing rather than a fixed protocol, is consistent with basic
    79	training-load principles and does not depend on accepting thread (b). The authors' own
    80	dosing statement: an athlete who benefits from MACS "should not assume that increased dosage
    81	will lead to further improvement. The contrary may well prove to be true" (p.214). Inference:
    82	do not use this entry to justify low-current "microcurrent" devices for performance or
    83	healing claims without independent, modern verification outside this book.

    86	(b) (glial cells acting like semiconductors, Nordenstrom's closed circuits, "resonant
    87	attunement" as the operative principle of MICS) are not treated here as independently
    88	replicated physiology, and this entry does not verify them against current literature. The
    89	Rodan (1978) and Cheng (1982) findings are animal and cell studies (chick cartilage, rat bone,

    91	"adaptation, growth and repair" effects in human athletes. The MICS safety claims (p.214,

    93	terms for this section.

    96	and safer than faradic stimulators should recognise that the claim is the authors' (citing
    97	Matteson & Eberhardt, 1985, p.213) and that its explanation rests on thread (b) (Becker,
    98	Nordenstrom, Pilla), and should keep the authors' own contraindications (p.214) in force
    99	whatever the device.

    39	produce greater strength, power and speed". This is sometimes called active
    40	electrostimulation (ES applied to active muscles), as distinct from passive
    41	electrostimulation (applied to relaxed muscles), the method most common in physical therapy
    42	(PDF p. 226, printed p. 215). (PDF p. 219, printed p. 208, "4.2.1 Electrostimulation"; PDF

    13	
    14	# Power Output Peaks and Declines With Load in a Barbell Jump, but Falls Steadily in a Seated Leg Extension (Captioned Leg-Press), Because of Elastic Energy
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The amount of work increases as the load raised by a weightlifter
    17	increases, but power output is not unidirectional. For lifting a barbell, power rises then
    18	falls once the load exceeds 66% of maximum (Chikvadze, 1961). "A similar result" holds for a
    19	jump with a barbell on the shoulders (Fig 4.2), where maximum power is at 30-40% of 1RM and
    20	maximal reactivity coefficient at 30-33% (PDF p. 227, printed p. 216). "Maximal dynamic
    21	force increases as the weight of the apparatus increases during the rapid increase in the
    22	movement time, mainly during the active thrust phase" (p.216). Verified against the page image (Fig 4.2, PDF p. 228,
    23	printed p. 217; readings from the figure, approximate): as load rises from 14% to 86% of max
    24	strength, Fmax and movement time rise; R (reactivity coefficient) peaks near 32%, power is
    25	highest across roughly 32-50%, and both fall at heavier loads. The authors attribute the rise
    26	in power and reactivity coefficient with increasing movement time to "the additional elastic
    27	energy accumulated in the muscles by absorbing the kinetic energy of the body and apparatus
    28	during the amortisation phase" (p.217).
    29	
    30	A contrasting experiment removes that elastic-energy source: "concentric lifting of
    31	progressively heavier weights (20, 40, 60, 80% of maximum) with seated leg extensions (from
    32	an initial knee angle of 110°)". Verified against the page image (Fig 4.3, PDF p. 228, printed
    33	p. 217): maximal force and movement time again increase with resistance "in an analogous way
    34	to jumps with a barbell", but "the extra elastic energy is lacking in this case, causing a
    35	progressive decrease in power output"; in the figure power falls steadily from 20% to 80%.
    36	The book labels Fig 4.3 "leg-press" in the caption but describes seated leg extensions from
    37	110° in the text (p.217); both are recorded. (PDF pp. 227-228, printed pp. 216-217, "4.2.2
    38	Resistance and Strength Training," Figs 4.2-4.3.)
    39	
    40	**Why it works** — The authors' stated mechanism is the presence or absence of an
    41	amortisation phase that stores and releases elastic energy: the jump-with-barbell condition
    42	includes it, so at moderate loads elastic-energy return can raise power and reactivity even
    43	as load rises, until added weight overwhelms that benefit; the seated leg-extension
    44	condition lacks the extra elastic energy, so power falls progressively as resistance climbs
    45	(p.217).
    46	
    47	**When to apply** — Use this as a caution when generalising a load-power relationship from
    48	one exercise type to another: a countermovement or stretch-shortening exercise can show
    49	power peaking at a submaximal load band (here, 30-40% of 1RM for maximal power, 30-33% for
    50	maximal reactivity, p.216), while a purely concentric exercise without amortisation (seated
    51	leg extension here) shows power declining as load rises. Inference: this is consistent with
    52	"optimal power load" testing protocols (e.g. jump squats across a load spectrum) finding a
    53	load band that maximises power. The 66% weightlifting threshold parallels the vault's
    54	two-thirds-of-maximum peak-power load for the competition squat (see
    55	[[claim--maximal-power-output-load-differs-lab-vs-competition-lift]]); the two figures come
    56	from different lifts and sources.
    57	
    58	**When NOT to apply** — This is single-lab, era-specific data (Chikvadze, 1961; Siff &
    59	Verkhoshansky, 1999 figures) on unspecified subjects; the percentages (66% for the
    60	weightlifting lift, 30-40% and 30-33% for the barbell jump) are illustrative for these
    61	protocols, not universal constants. Do not attach the 66% threshold to the barbell jump; the
    62	book gives it for the load raised by a weightlifter. Inference: load-power curves vary by
    63	exercise and population in the modern literature, which this passage does not address.
    64	
    65	**Example** — Inference: a coach programming loaded jump squats for maximal power output
    66	should expect the power curve to rise then fall across the load spectrum (Fig 4.2's
    67	pattern), and should not extrapolate that shape to a non-countermovement exercise like a
    68	seated leg extension, where the Fig 4.3 data show power declining steadily as load
    69	increases.
    70	
    71	**Related** — [[framework--force-time-curve-adaptation-pattern-by-movement-type]],
    72	[[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]] (a related but distinct
    73	reactivity-coefficient formulation from a different protocol, Ch3.2.1),
    74	[[claim--maximal-power-output-load-differs-lab-vs-competition-lift]] (Ch3.3.2, peak squat
    75	power at about two-thirds of maximum).

    13	
    14	# Inertial (Flywheel) and Elastic Resistance: Different Force Profiles From Free Weights, Each With Its Own Limitation
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors note that specialised equipment for training against a load's
    17	inertia (rather than its weight) is rarely used, despite the concept warranting more serious
    18	attention. Two solutions are given: applying force against a horizontal wheel or a
    19	suspended, pendulum-like load, or spinning a heavy flywheel ergometer with the arms or legs
    20	(Fig 4.4, elbow-flexion flywheel device, Verkhoshansky 1977). "In the first example, one can
    21	vary the amount of weight and in the second, the moment of inertia of the flywheel to affect
    22	speed of contraction." Flywheel ergometers can be used several ways: "accelerating against
    23	high inertia, using the heavy wheel to compel one to operate at a certain cadence, and
    24	opposing the angular momentum via eccentric muscle action to decelerate the wheel", with
    25	these methods combinable in short or mixed bursts. Elastic bands are treated as a separate
    26	case: resistance follows Hooke's Law (F = kx, where k is the spring constant and x is
    27	extension), so elastic force "begins from zero value and increases with movement range";
    28	therefore, the authors state, "elastic materials should not be used for developing
    29	starting-strength in ballistic movements or for developing explosive-strength". Inference:
    30	those qualities need force available from the very start of the movement, which elastics
    31	cannot supply. For strength-endurance over a selected range, however, an elastic band's
    32	length and elasticity can be chosen so its resistance changes minimally over the working
    33	range, a method "sometimes used by swimmers" to develop pulling strength-endurance (Fig 4.5,
    34	Verkhoshansky 1977). Resistance at "sticking points" can be reduced by moving toward the
    35	band's attachment point, or increased by moving away from it; resistance can also be varied
    36	across the full range by accelerating free weights through a decreasing-resistance portion
    37	of the lift (so-called Compensatory Acceleration Training, see
    38	[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]]) or by using dedicated variable-resistance
    39	machines. (PDF p. 230, printed p. 219, "4.2.2 Resistance and Strength Training," Figs
    40	4.4-4.5.)
    41	
    42	**Why it works** — For inertial devices, the authors' reasoning is that force against a
    43	load's inertia (F = ma) rather than its weight (F = m(g+a)): "Under conditions where
    44	strength is directed against the inertia of the load, predominantly the speed of muscular
    45	contraction is stimulated" (PDF p. 229, printed p. 218), so that in the inertia case "it
    46	is easy to appreciate the possibility for overcoming the opposing tendency between the
    47	weight of the load and the speed of muscular contraction" (p.219). Inference: the athlete
    48	trains speed of contraction against a resistance that is not present at rest and appears
    49	only once acceleration is applied. For elastic bands, the mechanism is Hooke's Law itself:
    50	resistance is proportional to extension, so it begins from zero at the start of the range
    51	and increases with range (p.219). Inference: this is the opposite loading curve from what
    52	ballistic and explosive-strength work needs.
    53	
    54	**When to apply** — Inference: use flywheel or inertial devices when the training goal is
    55	speed of muscular contraction against inertia specifically (per
    56	[[framework--two-force-regimes-overcoming-weight-vs-inertia]]), varying the moment of
    57	inertia (flywheel) or the amount of weight (pendulum or horizontal wheel) to adjust the
    58	demand, and consider "opposing the angular momentum via eccentric muscle action to
    59	decelerate the wheel" (p.219) as a separate use of the same device. Use elastic bands specifically for strength-endurance work over a selected range
    60	(the authors' cited example: swimmers' pulling strength-endurance), choosing band length and
    61	elasticity to minimise resistance variation across that range, and use position along the
    62	band (closer to or farther from the attachment) to manage sticking-point loading.
    63	
    64	**When NOT to apply** — Do not use elastic-band resistance alone for developing
    65	starting-strength or explosive-strength in ballistic movements; the authors state this
    66	directly, since Hooke's Law resistance is lowest exactly when ballistic/explosive movements
    67	most need force to be available. The flywheel and pendulum devices described are
    68	purpose-built or improvised apparatus (a 1992 University of the Witwatersrand student
    69	biomechanics project supplied the plyometric bench-press device shown nearby, Fig 4.6, PDF
    70	p. 231, printed p. 220, a related but separate kinetic-energy device); the authors give no standardised commercial
    71	specification for the flywheel or pendulum devices described here.
    72	
    73	**Example** — Inference: a swim coach building pulling strength-endurance with resistance
    74	bands, per the authors' own cited example, should select a band whose resistance changes
    75	little across the stroke's working range, rather than a stiffer band whose resistance would
    76	spike sharply near full extension; a sprint or jump coach chasing starting-strength or
    77	explosive-strength should not substitute elastic-band resistance for free weights or
    78	inertial-device training for that specific quality.
    79	
    80	**Related** — [[framework--two-force-regimes-overcoming-weight-vs-inertia]],
    81	[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]].
