    12	---
    13	
    14	# Two Ways Resistance Exercises Develop Force: Against a Load's Weight, or Against Its Inertia
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors distinguish resistance exercises by two different bases: first,
    17	by whether the working force is developed after preliminary muscular tension already equal
    18	to the apparatus's weight (e.g. the starting position of a squat or squat jump, where the
    19	legs and torso have already developed tension equal to the barbell's weight before the
    20	dynamic effort begins), or whether force is developed essentially from zero without
    21	appreciable preliminary tension (e.g. the snatch or clean-and-jerk, where the working force
    22	accelerating the bar starts from near zero). The first group does not appreciably influence
    23	the excitation-tension processes in the muscle and, depending on the weight used, chiefly
    24	develops either muscular strength or speed of contraction, but not the speed of switching
    25	from rest to active state; the second group has "simultaneous potential for developing
    26	dynamic strength, speed of movement and especially starting strength." Second, and
    27	separately, the authors classify exercises by which physical quantity the force is directed
    28	against: force against the weight of a load (F = m(g+a), determined by the load's mass and
    29	its acceleration against gravity, e.g. lifting a barbell), or force against the inertia of a
    30	load (F = ma, dependent only on the load's inertial force at a given acceleration, e.g.
    31	throwing, sprinting out of blocks, punching, where force acts roughly perpendicular to
    32	gravity). In the first (overcoming weight) case, muscular force first equals the load's
    33	weight (developed under virtually isometric conditions), then exceeds it as motion begins,
    34	producing "a large gradient of acceleration-strength." In the second (overcoming inertia)
    35	case, if friction and the resistance of the surroundings are excluded, movement begins with insignificant
    36	propulsive force, and further force changes depend entirely on the speed of muscular
    37	contraction, i.e. the muscle's simultaneous production of maximal strength and maximal speed
    38	of contraction. Consequently, resisting a load's weight primarily stimulates the strength
    39	component, while resisting a load's inertia primarily stimulates the speed of muscular
    40	contraction. (PDF pp. 229-230, printed pp. 218-219, "4.2.2 Resistance and Strength
    41	Training.")
    42	
    43	**Why it works** — The authors give the two force equations, F = m(g+a) against weight and
    44	F = ma against inertia (p.218), and state the cause of one difference: "The preliminary
    45	isometric muscular tension causes a large gradient of acceleration-strength" in the
    46	weight case, while in the inertia case "movement of the load begins with insignificant
    47	propulsive force" and further change is caused "wholly by the speed of muscular contraction"
    48	(PDF p. 229, printed p. 218). Inference: a muscle's neuromuscular demand differs between
    49	starting from a preloaded, isometric-like state and starting from rest against inertia
    50	alone.
    51	
    52	**When to apply** — Use the preliminary-tension distinction (loaded start vs start from
    53	zero) to classify which exercises target starting strength: from-zero exercises in the book
    54	are the snatch and clean-and-jerk, which the authors say have "simultaneous potential for
    55	developing dynamic strength, speed of movement and especially starting strength", while
    56	loaded-start exercises (squat, squat jump) do not appreciably train the speed with which
    57	muscles switch from rest to the active state (p.218). Inference: sprint starts, punches and
    58	throws are the book's examples of the separate inertia category, not of the from-zero group.
    59	Inference: use the weight-versus-inertia distinction to separate exercises meant to build
    60	strength against weight (heavy squats, deadlifts) from those meant to build speed of
    61	contraction against inertia (the book's examples: throwing, sprinting out of the starting
    62	blocks, punching, p.218).
    63	
    64	**When NOT to apply** — Inference: this is a biomechanical classification of the demand an
    65	exercise places on the neuromuscular system, not a training-volume or periodization
    66	prescription; the authors do not state how much of each type of exercise to program, only
    67	that the two types target different qualities. Do not assume every "explosive" exercise
    68	falls cleanly into one category; many sport movements (e.g. a jump shot, a football block)
    69	mix a loaded start with subsequent inertia-dominated acceleration, and this framework
    70	addresses the two idealized cases, not every blend.
    71	
    72	**Example** — The book's own examples: the squat and squat jump start with the legs and
    73	torso already tensed to the weight of the apparatus; the snatch and clean-and-jerk develop
    74	the working force "practically from zero"; throwing, sprinting out of the starting blocks and
    75	punching are force against inertia, acting "approximately perpendicular to the gravitational
    76	force" (p.218). Inference: a punch (force against inertia) and a back squat (loaded start,
    77	force against weight) therefore sit at opposite ends of both classifications. Inference: a
    78	broad jump is mixed; vertical support against body weight means it is not a pure inertia
    79	case.
    80	
    81	**Related** — [[claim--power-output-peaks-then-declines-with-load-jump-vs-leg-press]],
    82	[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]] (Ch1, a related point that free-weight
    83	resistance already varies with acceleration per Newton's second law).

    13	
    14	# Four Ways to Stimulate Working Muscular Tension, and How They Map to the Rest of the Chapter
    15	
    16	**What it is** — External muscular force is a product of voluntary effort, but voluntary
    17	effort alone has limits; the authors classify how "stimulation of working force" is
    18	supplied from outside that voluntary effort into four basic types: (1) muscular tension
    19	produced by voluntary effort against external resistance, where the moving load's
    20	resistance "accelerates and regulates the effector impulses to the muscles"; (2)
    21	stimulation by the kinetic energy of a falling object or the body, where "the effort is
    22	primarily reflexive"; (3) stimulation caused primarily by voluntary effort under conditions
    23	where additional external mechanical stimulation is absent or limited; and (4) stimulation
    24	of muscle "elicited or intensified involuntarily by means of external electrical current."
    25	The authors group the first two as dynamic work and the third as isometric work. "An
    26	increase in stimulation is realised in the first case by increasing the velocity of the
    27	preliminary fall of the body or load, and by mobilising the athlete's voluntary resources in
    28	the third" (PDF p. 219, printed p. 208). The book assigns fall velocity to "the first case";
    29	in context this reads as a slip for the second (falling-body) type. Recorded as written.
    30	Voluntary effort plays an important role in the first case, but its influence in the second
    31	is "insignificant"; the braking or amortisation mechanism causes a protective effector
    32	response more rapidly than a voluntary sequence of actions, and "this mechanism forms the
    33	foundation of plyometric training (5.2.4)" (p.208; see
    34	[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]). Inference: the four types map onto
    35	the chapter's structure: type (4) as 4.2.1 Electrostimulation, type (1) as 4.2.2 Resistance
    36	and Strength Training, type (2) as 4.2.3 Kinetic Energy and Strength Processes, and type (3)
    37	as 4.2.4 Isometric Training; the book does not state this mapping. (PDF pp. 218-219, printed
    38	pp. 207-208, "4.2 Different Means of Strength Development.")
    39	
    40	**Why it works** — The authors' stated reason: afferent impulses elicited by mechanical
    41	stimulation inform the central nervous system about the strength of the external
    42	influence evoking muscular tension, and "the greater the intensity of the external
    43	stimulus, the greater the muscle effector discharge, and the larger the external work
    44	produced" (PDF p. 218, printed p. 207). Inference: this is a general afferent-feedback framing rather than a
    45	mechanism specific to any one of the four types; the chapter's later sections give more
    46	detailed, type-specific mechanisms (e.g. elastic energy storage for the falling-body case,
    47	gradual overload for the resistance case).
    48	
    49	**When to apply** — Inference: use this as an organizing checklist when auditing a program's strength
    50	means: does a given exercise stimulate tension primarily through external resistance,
    51	through absorbed kinetic energy (a fall or catch), through sustained voluntary effort with
    52	little external aid (isometric), or through externally applied electrical current? Mixing
    53	means from more than one category (e.g. resistance plus electrostimulation) is a distinct
    54	programming decision from staying within one category, and the chapter's later sections
    55	(4.2.1 Electrostimulation, "Sports Functional Electrostimulation") discuss combining
    56	categories explicitly.
    57	
    58	**When NOT to apply** — Inference: this is the book's own convenience classification for
    59	organizing chapter 4.2, not a claim that these four mechanisms are mutually exclusive
    60	within a single exercise (a depth jump followed by a jump, for example, combines kinetic-
    61	energy stimulation with subsequent voluntary resistance work). Do not treat the four-way
    62	split as a measurement protocol; it carries no associated testing method here.
    63	
    64	**Example** — Inference: a coach comparing a paused back squat (voluntary effort against
    65	external resistance, type 1), a depth jump (kinetic energy of a fall, type 2), a wall sit
    66	(sustained voluntary isometric effort, type 3), and a quadriceps NMES session (external
    67	electrical current, type 4) is comparing four different stimulation mechanisms for the same
    68	target muscle group, each covered by a different subsection of this chapter. This example
    69	is not in the source.
    70	
    71	**Related** — [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] (Ch1, the falling-body
    72	mechanism this framework's type 2 builds on); [[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]]
    73	(Ch1, the mechanical regimes -concentric, eccentric, isometric- this framework's types map
    74	onto at the muscle-action level, a distinct but adjacent classification).

    53	load band that maximises power. The 66% weightlifting threshold parallels the vault's
    54	two-thirds-of-maximum peak-power load for the competition squat (see
    55	[[claim--maximal-power-output-load-differs-lab-vs-competition-lift]]); the two figures come
    56	from different lifts and sources.

    58	**When NOT to apply** — This is single-lab, era-specific data (Chikvadze, 1961; Siff &
    59	Verkhoshansky, 1999 figures) on unspecified subjects; the percentages (66% for the
    60	weightlifting lift, 30-40% and 30-33% for the barbell jump) are illustrative for these
    61	protocols, not universal constants. Do not attach the 66% threshold to the barbell jump; the
    62	book gives it for the load raised by a weightlifter. Inference: load-power curves vary by
    63	exercise and population in the modern literature, which this passage does not address.

    66	should expect the power curve to rise then fall across the load spectrum (Fig 4.2's

    13	
    14	# Inertial (Flywheel) and Elastic Resistance: Different Force Profiles From Free Weights, Each With Its Own Limitation
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors note that specialised equipment for training against a load's
    17	inertia (rather than its weight) is rarely used, despite the concept warranting more serious
    18	attention. Two solutions are given: applying force against a horizontal wheel or a
    19	suspended, pendulum-like load, or spinning a heavy flywheel ergometer with the arms or legs
    20	(Fig 4.4, elbow-flexion flywheel device, Verkhoshansky 1977). "In the first example, one can
    21	vary the amount of weight and in the second, the moment of inertia of the flywheel to affect
    22	speed of contraction." Flywheel ergometers can be used several ways: "accelerating against
    23	high inertia, using the heavy wheel to compel one to operate at a certain cadence, and
    24	opposing the angular momentum via eccentric muscle action to decelerate the wheel", with
    25	these methods combinable in short or mixed bursts. Elastic bands are treated as a separate
    26	case: resistance follows Hooke's Law (F = kx, where k is the spring constant and x is
    27	extension), so elastic force "begins from zero value and increases with movement range";
    28	therefore, the authors state, "elastic materials should not be used for developing
    29	starting-strength in ballistic movements or for developing explosive-strength". Inference:
    30	those qualities need force available from the very start of the movement, which elastics
    31	cannot supply. For strength-endurance over a selected range, however, an elastic band's
    32	length and elasticity can be chosen so its resistance changes minimally over the working
    33	range, a method "sometimes used by swimmers" to develop pulling strength-endurance (Fig 4.5,
    34	Verkhoshansky 1977). Resistance at "sticking points" can be reduced by moving toward the
    35	band's attachment point, or increased by moving away from it; resistance can also be varied
    36	across the full range by accelerating free weights through a decreasing-resistance portion
    37	of the lift (so-called Compensatory Acceleration Training, see
    38	[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]]) or by using dedicated variable-resistance
    39	machines. (PDF p. 230, printed p. 219, "4.2.2 Resistance and Strength Training," Figs
    40	4.4-4.5.)
    41	
    42	**Why it works** — For inertial devices, the authors' reasoning is that force against a
    43	load's inertia (F = ma) rather than its weight (F = m(g+a)): "Under conditions where
    44	strength is directed against the inertia of the load, predominantly the speed of muscular
    45	contraction is stimulated" (PDF p. 229, printed p. 218), so that in the inertia case "it
    46	is easy to appreciate the possibility for overcoming the opposing tendency between the
    47	weight of the load and the speed of muscular contraction" (p.219). Inference: the athlete
    48	trains speed of contraction against a resistance that is not present at rest and appears
    49	only once acceleration is applied. For elastic bands, the mechanism is Hooke's Law itself:
    50	resistance is proportional to extension, so it begins from zero at the start of the range
    51	and increases with range (p.219). Inference: this is the opposite loading curve from what
    52	ballistic and explosive-strength work needs.
    53	
    54	**When to apply** — Inference: use flywheel or inertial devices when the training goal is
    55	speed of muscular contraction against inertia specifically (per
    56	[[framework--two-force-regimes-overcoming-weight-vs-inertia]]), varying the moment of
    57	inertia (flywheel) or the amount of weight (pendulum or horizontal wheel) to adjust the
    58	demand, and consider "opposing the angular momentum via eccentric muscle action to
    59	decelerate the wheel" (p.219) as a separate use of the same device. Use elastic bands specifically for strength-endurance work over a selected range
    60	(the authors' cited example: swimmers' pulling strength-endurance), choosing band length and
    61	elasticity to minimise resistance variation across that range, and use position along the
    62	band (closer to or farther from the attachment) to manage sticking-point loading.
    63	
    64	**When NOT to apply** — Do not use elastic-band resistance alone for developing
    65	starting-strength or explosive-strength in ballistic movements; the authors state this
    66	directly, since Hooke's Law resistance is lowest exactly when ballistic/explosive movements
    67	most need force to be available. The flywheel and pendulum devices described are
    68	purpose-built or improvised apparatus (a 1992 University of the Witwatersrand student
    69	biomechanics project supplied the plyometric bench-press device shown nearby, Fig 4.6, PDF
    70	p. 231, printed p. 220, a related but separate kinetic-energy device); the authors give no standardised commercial
    71	specification for the flywheel or pendulum devices described here.
    72	
    73	**Example** — Inference: a swim coach building pulling strength-endurance with resistance
    74	bands, per the authors' own cited example, should select a band whose resistance changes
    75	little across the stroke's working range, rather than a stiffer band whose resistance would
    76	spike sharply near full extension; a sprint or jump coach chasing starting-strength or
    77	explosive-strength should not substitute elastic-band resistance for free weights or
    78	inertial-device training for that specific quality.
    79	
    80	**Related** — [[framework--two-force-regimes-overcoming-weight-vs-inertia]],
    81	[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]].

    13	
    14	# Two Ways Resistance Exercises Develop Force: Against a Load's Weight, or Against Its Inertia
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors distinguish resistance exercises by two different bases: first,
    17	by whether the working force is developed after preliminary muscular tension already equal
    18	to the apparatus's weight (e.g. the starting position of a squat or squat jump, where the
    19	legs and torso have already developed tension equal to the barbell's weight before the
    20	dynamic effort begins), or whether force is developed essentially from zero without
    21	appreciable preliminary tension (e.g. the snatch or clean-and-jerk, where the working force
    22	accelerating the bar starts from near zero). The first group does not appreciably influence
    23	the excitation-tension processes in the muscle and, depending on the weight used, chiefly
    24	develops either muscular strength or speed of contraction, but not the speed of switching
    25	from rest to active state; the second group has "simultaneous potential for developing
    26	dynamic strength, speed of movement and especially starting strength." Second, and
    27	separately, the authors classify exercises by which physical quantity the force is directed
    28	against: force against the weight of a load (F = m(g+a), determined by the load's mass and
    29	its acceleration against gravity, e.g. lifting a barbell), or force against the inertia of a
    30	load (F = ma, dependent only on the load's inertial force at a given acceleration, e.g.
    31	throwing, sprinting out of blocks, punching, where force acts roughly perpendicular to
    32	gravity). In the first (overcoming weight) case, muscular force first equals the load's
    33	weight (developed under virtually isometric conditions), then exceeds it as motion begins,
    34	producing "a large gradient of acceleration-strength." In the second (overcoming inertia)
    35	case, if friction and the resistance of the surroundings are excluded, movement begins with insignificant
    36	propulsive force, and further force changes depend entirely on the speed of muscular
    37	contraction, i.e. the muscle's simultaneous production of maximal strength and maximal speed
    38	of contraction. Consequently, resisting a load's weight primarily stimulates the strength
    39	component, while resisting a load's inertia primarily stimulates the speed of muscular
    40	contraction. (PDF pp. 229-230, printed pp. 218-219, "4.2.2 Resistance and Strength
    41	Training.")
    42	
    43	**Why it works** — The authors give the two force equations, F = m(g+a) against weight and
    44	F = ma against inertia (p.218), and state the cause of one difference: "The preliminary
    45	isometric muscular tension causes a large gradient of acceleration-strength" in the
    46	weight case, while in the inertia case "movement of the load begins with insignificant
    47	propulsive force" and further change is caused "wholly by the speed of muscular contraction"
    48	(PDF p. 229, printed p. 218). Inference: a muscle's neuromuscular demand differs between
    49	starting from a preloaded, isometric-like state and starting from rest against inertia
    50	alone.
    51	
    52	**When to apply** — Use the preliminary-tension distinction (loaded start vs start from
    53	zero) to classify which exercises target starting strength: from-zero exercises in the book
    54	are the snatch and clean-and-jerk, which the authors say have "simultaneous potential for
    55	developing dynamic strength, speed of movement and especially starting strength", while
    56	loaded-start exercises (squat, squat jump) do not appreciably train the speed with which
    57	muscles switch from rest to the active state (p.218). Inference: sprint starts, punches and
    58	throws are the book's examples of the separate inertia category, not of the from-zero group.
    59	Inference: use the weight-versus-inertia distinction to separate exercises meant to build
    60	strength against weight (heavy squats, deadlifts) from those meant to build speed of
    61	contraction against inertia (the book's examples: throwing, sprinting out of the starting
    62	blocks, punching, p.218).
    63	
    64	**When NOT to apply** — Inference: this is a biomechanical classification of the demand an
    65	exercise places on the neuromuscular system, not a training-volume or periodization
    66	prescription; the authors do not state how much of each type of exercise to program, only
    67	that the two types target different qualities. Do not assume every "explosive" exercise
    68	falls cleanly into one category; many sport movements (e.g. a jump shot, a football block)
    69	mix a loaded start with subsequent inertia-dominated acceleration, and this framework
    70	addresses the two idealized cases, not every blend.
    71	
    72	**Example** — The book's own examples: the squat and squat jump start with the legs and
    73	torso already tensed to the weight of the apparatus; the snatch and clean-and-jerk develop
    74	the working force "practically from zero"; throwing, sprinting out of the starting blocks and
    75	punching are force against inertia, acting "approximately perpendicular to the gravitational
    76	force" (p.218). Inference: a punch (force against inertia) and a back squat (loaded start,
    77	force against weight) therefore sit at opposite ends of both classifications. Inference: a
    78	broad jump is mixed; vertical support against body weight means it is not a pure inertia
    79	case.
    80	
    81	**Related** — [[claim--power-output-peaks-then-declines-with-load-jump-vs-leg-press]],
    82	[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]] (Ch1, a related point that free-weight
    83	resistance already varies with acceleration per Newton's second law).

    13	
    14	# Four Ways to Stimulate Working Muscular Tension, and How They Map to the Rest of the Chapter
    15	
    16	**What it is** — External muscular force is a product of voluntary effort, but voluntary
    17	effort alone has limits; the authors classify how "stimulation of working force" is
    18	supplied from outside that voluntary effort into four basic types: (1) muscular tension
    19	produced by voluntary effort against external resistance, where the moving load's
    20	resistance "accelerates and regulates the effector impulses to the muscles"; (2)
    21	stimulation by the kinetic energy of a falling object or the body, where "the effort is
    22	primarily reflexive"; (3) stimulation caused primarily by voluntary effort under conditions
    23	where additional external mechanical stimulation is absent or limited; and (4) stimulation
    24	of muscle "elicited or intensified involuntarily by means of external electrical current."
    25	The authors group the first two as dynamic work and the third as isometric work. "An
    26	increase in stimulation is realised in the first case by increasing the velocity of the
    27	preliminary fall of the body or load, and by mobilising the athlete's voluntary resources in
    28	the third" (PDF p. 219, printed p. 208). The book assigns fall velocity to "the first case";
    29	in context this reads as a slip for the second (falling-body) type. Recorded as written.
    30	Voluntary effort plays an important role in the first case, but its influence in the second
    31	is "insignificant"; the braking or amortisation mechanism causes a protective effector
    32	response more rapidly than a voluntary sequence of actions, and "this mechanism forms the
    33	foundation of plyometric training (5.2.4)" (p.208; see
    34	[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]). Inference: the four types map onto
    35	the chapter's structure: type (4) as 4.2.1 Electrostimulation, type (1) as 4.2.2 Resistance
    36	and Strength Training, type (2) as 4.2.3 Kinetic Energy and Strength Processes, and type (3)
    37	as 4.2.4 Isometric Training; the book does not state this mapping. (PDF pp. 218-219, printed
    38	pp. 207-208, "4.2 Different Means of Strength Development.")
    39	
    40	**Why it works** — The authors' stated reason: afferent impulses elicited by mechanical
    41	stimulation inform the central nervous system about the strength of the external
    42	influence evoking muscular tension, and "the greater the intensity of the external
    43	stimulus, the greater the muscle effector discharge, and the larger the external work
    44	produced" (PDF p. 218, printed p. 207). Inference: this is a general afferent-feedback framing rather than a
    45	mechanism specific to any one of the four types; the chapter's later sections give more
    46	detailed, type-specific mechanisms (e.g. elastic energy storage for the falling-body case,
    47	gradual overload for the resistance case).
    48	
    49	**When to apply** — Inference: use this as an organizing checklist when auditing a program's strength
    50	means: does a given exercise stimulate tension primarily through external resistance,
    51	through absorbed kinetic energy (a fall or catch), through sustained voluntary effort with
    52	little external aid (isometric), or through externally applied electrical current? Mixing
    53	means from more than one category (e.g. resistance plus electrostimulation) is a distinct
    54	programming decision from staying within one category, and the chapter's later sections
    55	(4.2.1 Electrostimulation, "Sports Functional Electrostimulation") discuss combining
    56	categories explicitly.
    57	
    58	**When NOT to apply** — Inference: this is the book's own convenience classification for
    59	organizing chapter 4.2, not a claim that these four mechanisms are mutually exclusive
    60	within a single exercise (a depth jump followed by a jump, for example, combines kinetic-
    61	energy stimulation with subsequent voluntary resistance work). Do not treat the four-way
    62	split as a measurement protocol; it carries no associated testing method here.
    63	
    64	**Example** — Inference: a coach comparing a paused back squat (voluntary effort against
    65	external resistance, type 1), a depth jump (kinetic energy of a fall, type 2), a wall sit
    66	(sustained voluntary isometric effort, type 3), and a quadriceps NMES session (external
    67	electrical current, type 4) is comparing four different stimulation mechanisms for the same
    68	target muscle group, each covered by a different subsection of this chapter. This example
    69	is not in the source.
    70	
    71	**Related** — [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] (Ch1, the falling-body
    72	mechanism this framework's type 2 builds on); [[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]]
    73	(Ch1, the mechanical regimes -concentric, eccentric, isometric- this framework's types map
    74	onto at the muscle-action level, a distinct but adjacent classification).

    14	# The Optimal Depth-Jump Drop Height Is 0.75-1.15 Metres: Maximal Power at the Low End, Maximal Force at the High End
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Fig 4.7 (PDF p. 232, printed p. 221; Verkhoshansky, 1977) plots force, in
    17	bodyweights, against time for three vertical jumps: (1) jumping from rest from a low squat,
    18	(2) the usual jump with a dip or amortisation phase, (3) a jump after a depth jump from
    19	0.4 m. The caption gives jump heights of 0.67 m, 0.74 m and 0.80 m respectively. Verified
    20	against the page image (readings from the figure, approximate): curve 1 peaks early, about
    21	1.4-1.5 BW at about 0.08-0.1 s, and ends about 0.3 s; curve 2 first drops below bodyweight
    22	(about 0.6 BW at about 0.15 s), then peaks about 1.4 BW at about 0.5 s and ends about 0.8 s;
    23	curve 3 peaks about 3 BW at about 0.1 s and ends about 0.25 s. Curves 1 and 2 have similar
    24	peaks, and curve 2's is the later; only curve 3 is clearly higher and earlier.
    25	
    26	Depth jumps from a range of drop heights (Fig 4.10, PDF p. 234, printed p. 223): the text
    27	states that "maximal force (Fmax) increases up to a height of 1.15 metres, then diminishes
    28	sharply, while movement time begins by changing insignificantly, then increasing sharply.
    29	Maximum power and reactivity are achieved using a drop height of approximately 0.75 metres"
    30	(PDF p. 233, printed p. 222). Verified against the page image (approximate): Fmax peaks near
    31	1.1-1.15 m and falls sharply to 1.55 m; the figure also carries a Power curve, not named in
    32	the caption, peaking about 0.75 m; RC peaks about 0.8 m; ground contact time t dips slightly
    33	to a minimum about 0.75 m, then rises sharply. The authors conclude that the optimal range of
    34	depth jumping for stimulating muscular activity is 0.75-1.15 metres, "because at the lower
    35	end of this range the muscles are working at maximal power and at the upper end they are
    36	working at maximal dynamic force". This finding "forms the basis for the recommendations for
    37	using depth jumps in the training of advanced jumpers (Verkhoshansky 1963, 1964, 1966)",
    38	though it is "preferable to err on the conservative side of using considerably lower jump
    39	heights with anyone who is unused to this type of training and to strictly limit the volume
    40	of this type of 'shock' training" (p.222).
    41	
    42	The book states the result past 1.15 m two ways. The Fig 4.10 text says Fmax "diminishes
    43	sharply" past 1.15 m; the next paragraph says further increases in height "significantly
    44	decrease the magnitude of the dynamic parameters of the take-off", support time increases
    45	quickly because the eccentric-concentric switch is lengthened, and "the maximum dynamic force
    46	of take-off and the speed of muscular contraction stabilise and do not increase any further"
    47	(p.222). The figure shows a sharp fall. Both are recorded; `contested` is set for this
    48	internal contradiction. The take-off comprises amortisation (kinetic energy of the fall
    49	absorbed, with increasing depth of knee flexion) and the thrust proper (fairly constant
    50	speed of muscle contraction) (p.222).
    51	
    52	Loaded depth jumps (Fig 4.9, PDF p. 234, printed p. 223; the caption is on the page image, not
    53	in the text layer): after an unloaded depth jump (M = mass of athlete) and with an extra 10,
    54	20, 30 and 40 kg. Verified against the page image: rebound height h2, force F and RC fall and
    55	contact time t rises as load increases from M to M+40 kg. The text groups Figs 4.9 and 4.10
    56	as showing the same tendency as the thrown-load experiment "under other conditions, although
    57	these have their own peculiarities", and concludes "it is not beneficial to increase kinetic
    58	energy by use of heavier loads" (p.222; see
    59	[[claim--thrown-load-height-decreases-with-load-increases-with-drop-height]]). (PDF pp.
    60	232-234, printed pp. 221-223, "4.2.3 Kinetic Energy and Strength Processes," Figs 4.7, 4.9,
    61	4.10.)
    62	
    63	**Why it works** — The authors' stated mechanism is elastic-energy storage during
    64	amortisation and its release in the thrust (see
    65	[[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]]), and for heights
    66	past the optimum the lengthened switch from eccentric to concentric work (p.222). Inference:
    67	at greater drop heights more of the force capacity may go to braking, which would fit force
    68	rising to 1.15 m while power and reactivity peak earlier; the book does not state this.
    69	
    70	**When to apply** — For advanced jumpers (Verkhoshansky 1963, 1964, 1966; p.222), use about
    71	0.75 m when the training goal is maximal power and reactivity, and up to about 1.15 m when
    72	the goal is maximal dynamic force, per this protocol. For athletes unused to depth-jump
    73	training, start considerably lower and strictly limit volume, per the authors' caution.
    74	Inference: this gives a citable historical anchor for programming depth-jump height, distinct
    75	from the fixed 0.4 m depth-jump reactivity test already in this library (see
    76	[[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]]).
    77	
    78	**When NOT to apply** — This is single-lab, era-specific data (Verkhoshansky, 1963-1977) on
    79	an unspecified population (the authors do not state training age, sport or sample size for
    80	the drop-height experiment); do not apply 0.75 m and 1.15 m to every athlete without
    81	accounting for training age, technical competency and bodymass, which the authors flag. Do
    82	not cite the book as saying force merely plateaus past 1.15 m, or merely falls: it says both
    83	(p.222). Do not conflate this variable drop-height range with the fixed 0.4 m reactivity test
    84	(see Related).
    85	
    86	**Example** — The book's own example is the Fig 4.7, 4.9 and 4.10 data described above; no
    87	further example is added here.
    88

    91	[[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]] (Ch3.2.1, a related but distinct
    92	fixed 0.4 m depth-jump protocol measuring reactive ability rather than optimal training drop
    93	height),
    94	[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]].

    14	# Heavier Falling Loads Reduce Throw Height; Higher Falls Help Only Light Loads (Kinetic-Energy Throw Experiment)
    15	
    16	**What it is** — A laboratory stand measured "the height attained by a load when a subject
    17	threw it upward after it had first fallen from some height (from 0.5 to 3.0 metres)" (PDF
    18	p. 232, printed p. 221). The load was 3.3, 6.6, 9.9 and 13.3% of the subject's maximum
    19	isometric strength (Po) (Verkhoshansky, 1977); the figure labels the third load "10% Po"
    20	where the text says 9.9% (PDF p. 233, printed p. 222). The authors summarise: "an increase in
    21	kinetic energy caused by an increase in the mass of the load decreases the height to which a
    22	load is thrown, but an increase in the distance through which a load falls increases the
    23	height to which it is thrown (Fig 4.8a)" (p.222).
    24	
    25	Fig 4.8a as read (PDF p. 233, printed p. 222; readings from the figure, approximate): the
    26	x-axis (drop height h1) runs from 0 to 3 m, although the text gives 0.5-3.0 m. Only the 3.3%
    27	Po curve rises throughout, from about 108 to about 128 cm. The 6.6% curve peaks about 108 cm

    14	# Stimulating Muscle by Absorbing a Fall's Kinetic Energy: The Mechanics and Five Claimed Advantages Over Weighted Resistance
    15	
    16	**What it is** — When a training device such as a barbell falls from a height and the
    17	athlete's task is to actively stop it, then quickly thrust it upward (Fig 4.6, a purpose-built
    18	plyometric bench-press device from a 1992 University of the Witwatersrand student
    19	biomechanics project), the total muscular working force developed by eccentric amortisation
    20	followed by active concentric work can be calculated as F = m(V1^2/2S1 + g) + m(V2^2/2S2 +
    21	g), where V1 and V2 are the barbell's velocity at displacements S1 and S2 (derived from V^2 =
    22	u^2 + 2as). Much of the falling apparatus's kinetic energy converts, during the amortisation
    23	phase, into elastic energy used in the subsequent concentric work; excluding losses such as
    24	heat and viscous damping as a first approximation, this elastic energy equals the kinetic
    25	energy at the end of the fall (KE = mgh, where h is the fall height). Muscular force at the
    26	eccentric-to-concentric switch is greater for a shorter amortisation phase and shorter
    27	braking time, provided the goal is to thrust the apparatus at maximum speed immediately
    28	after stopping it. The authors state the external mechanical stimulus here is "not so much
    29	the weight (and its force of inertia) as the energy accumulated after its free-fall,"
    30	distinguishing this from ordinary weighted resistance (see
    31	[[framework--two-force-regimes-overcoming-weight-vs-inertia]]). Drawing on the vertical-jump
    32	data in Fig 4.7 (see
    33	[[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]), the authors list five claimed
    34	advantages of this stimulation method: (1) it develops maximal dynamic force very rapidly;
    35	(2) the magnitude of that maximum is significantly larger than other methods produce; (3) a
    36	large maximal force is achieved without additional resistance; (4) the eccentric-to-concentric
    37	switch happens far more rapidly than with other methods; (5) the elastic energy accumulated
    38	without additional resistance produces greater power and faster contraction in the thrust
    39	phase, inferred from the greater jump height reached. (PDF pp. 231-232, printed pp. 220-221,
    40	"4.2.3 Kinetic Energy and Strength Processes," Fig 4.6.)
    41

    43	the amortisation phase (the same mechanism underlying the shock method, see

1. Phys Ther. 2005 Apr;85(4):358-64.

Recruitment patterns in human skeletal muscle during electrical stimulation.

Gregory CM(1), Bickel CS.

Author information:
(1)Department of Physical Therapy, University of Florida, Room 1142, HPNP Bldg, 
101 S Newell Dr, Gainesville, FL 32610, USA. cgregory@phhp.ufl.edu

Electromyostimulation (EMS) incorporates the use of electrical current to 
activate skeletal muscle and facilitate contraction. It is commonly used in 
clinical settings to mimic voluntary contractions and enhance the rehabilitation 
of human skeletal muscles. Although the beneficial effects of EMS are widely 
accepted, discrepancies concerning the specific responses to EMS versus 
voluntary actions exist. The unique effects of EMS have been attributed to 
several mechanisms, most notably a reversal of the recruitment pattern typically 
associated with voluntary muscle activation. This perspective outlines the 
authors' contention that electrical stimulation recruits motor units in a 
nonselective, spatially fixed, and temporally synchronous pattern. Furthermore, 
it synthesizes the evidence that supports the contention that this recruitment 
pattern contributes to increased muscle fatigue when compared with voluntary 
actions. The authors believe the majority of evidence suggests that EMS-induced 
motor unit recruitment is nonselective and that muscle fibers are recruited 
without obvious sequencing related to fiber types.

PMID: 15794706 [Indexed for MEDLINE]

# Review: Supertraining 4.2 intro and 4.2.1-4.2.3 (round 2, Opus)

Reviewer: Claude Opus, independent round-2 reviewer, 2026-09-27. I did not write these entries or their fixes. Read-only on the entries and sources; this file is the only write.
Inputs read in full: `docs/ATOMIZE_BRIEF.md`, `staging/review_book_prompt.md`, `docs/method-baseline.md` (force-plate section, line 61), `staging/review_supertraining_ch4-2a_opus.md`, `staging/fixes_supertraining_ch4-2a_applied.md`, all 15 scoped entries, and `_book.md` lines 150-201.
Source: `staging/books/supertraining-6th-expanded.pdf`. Locators are 0-based PDF idx = printed + 11.

## Pages opened and checks run

- **Text layer**, PyMuPDF, idx 217-235 (printed 206-224), read in full.
- **Page images** opened by me: idx 219 (p.208: four-mechanisms "first case" sentence, Kots "have established", Ratov intro); idx 220 (p.209: Kots/Canadians, Reding third person, "continue to disagree"); idx 225 (p.214: MICS "generally entirely safe", MACS "Under no circumstances", contraindications); idx 226 (p.215: Ratov, "Work that I witnessed", "applied to the author by Serge Reding", flip-flop pattern, 5-10 min limit, MICS "cannot produce overtraining or injury"); idx 228 full page plus 300 dpi crops of Fig 4.2 and Fig 4.3; idx 230 (Figs 4.4, 4.5); idx 232 full page plus a crop of Fig 4.7; idx 233 full page plus crops of Fig 4.8a and 4.8b; idx 234 full page plus crops of Fig 4.9 and Fig 4.10.
- **Figure readings confirmed** (what the entries now say matches the image): Fig 4.2 (Fmax and Time rise; R peaks near 32%; Power flat-topped about 32-50%, then falls; caption also cites Siff & Verkhoshansky 1999); Fig 4.3 (power falls steadily 20-80%); Fig 4.7 (curve 1 about 1.45 BW at about 0.08-0.1 s, ends about 0.3 s; curve 2 dips to about 0.6 BW, peaks about 1.4 BW near 0.5 s, ends 0.8 s; curve 3 about 3 BW near 0.1 s, ends about 0.25 s); Fig 4.8a (only 3.3% Po rises throughout, about 108 to 128 cm; 6.6%, 10%, 13.3% rise to a peak at about 1-2 m, then fall; lighter loads are higher at every drop height); Fig 4.8b (bold per-load curves rise with KE; 13.3% rises about 1.3 to 2.0 near 15 J, dips to about 1.8 at 20 J; the thin arcs are consistent with equal drop heights, since the 0.5 arc meets 3.3% near 1.5 J and 13.3% near 6 J, a 4x KE ratio for a 4x mass); Fig 4.9 (caption: unloaded, then extra 10-40 kg; h2, F, RC fall, t rises); Fig 4.10 (Fmax peaks about 1.0-1.15 m and falls sharply to 1.55 m; Power, not in the caption, peaks about 0.75 m; RC peaks about 0.8 m; t lowest about 0.75 m, then rises sharply).
- **Gregory & Bickel 2005** confirmed via NCBI E-utilities (PubMed record 15794706): Gregory CM, Bickel CS. "Recruitment patterns in human skeletal muscle during electrical stimulation." Phys Ther 2005;85(4):358-64. It is a perspective article. Its abstract: "This perspective outlines the authors' contention that electrical stimulation recruits motor units in a nonselective, spatially fixed, and temporally synchronous pattern", and it names "a reversal of the recruitment pattern" as the mechanism it disputes. The entry's wording and quote match. It stays.
- **Dupuy 2018** vault entry line 52: "Stretching and electrostimulation did not significantly improve DOMS or fatigue in the pooled analyses. [p. 11]". Matches both entries that cite it.
- **Links:** every `[[link]]` in the 15 files resolves (staging library or vault library, scripted check). No wrapped wikilinks.
- **Dashes, headers, history:** scripted check. No U+2014 outside the six `**Header** —` lines, no U+2013, all six headers present in all 15 files, and no review-history words.
- **Old strings:** every Old string below was checked by script against the current file bytes. Each occurs exactly once, and all files use LF line endings.
- **Lint** (`PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8 python scripts/lint_library.py staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky`, run from WT):

```
supertraining--verkhoshansky/_book.md: body em dash lines [12, 114, 115]
TOTAL ISSUES: 1
```

That one finding is the known `_book.md` title/table false positive.

## Rulings on the fixer's "Disagreements with the review"

1. **Depth-jump `contested`: overruled; set `supported` (C17).** This is the criterion I apply to all three confidence questions, for this and later batches. An internal contradiction sets `contested` when it disputes the entry's title claim. When it touches only a secondary detail, it is recorded in the body. The p.222 contradiction ("diminishes sharply" vs "stabilise and do not increase any further") concerns only what happens past 1.15 m, and both readings agree that force does not rise past 1.15 m. The claim (optimal range 0.75-1.15 m, power at the low end, force at the high end) is stated once, consistently, and matches Fig 4.10. A `contested` label would tell a reader the range itself is disputed, which the book does not show. Keep both statements in the body.
2. **Thrown-load `contested`: upheld.** By the same criterion, the text-vs-figure disagreement concerns half of the title claim itself: whether a higher fall raises throw height. The text says it does; Fig 4.8a says it does only up to about 1-2 m for three of four loads. The reason is stated in the body. However, the title the fixer took from round 1 is false on the figure (C19).
3. **Fig 4.8b 13.3% curve**: the fixer's reading is correct (rises about 1.3 to about 2.0 near 15 J, then dips to about 1.8). Labelling the thin-arc identification Inference is correct; the 4x KE check above supports it.
4. **Fig 4.7 curve 1 peak "about 0.08-0.1 s"**: accepted.
5. **Ward & Shkuratova 2002 not cited**: accepted. Record as an unresolved spot: that abstract gives Kots's claimed gains as "up to 40%", against the book's "more than 20%" (p.209). Not a required change.
6. **Gregory & Bickel cited without journal**: accepted then. It is now confirmed, so C8 (optional) adds the journal and article type.
7. **MACS/MICS mainstream-status judgment left as Inference**: accepted. But the entry's `contested` still has no stated reason (C9).
8. **Fixer's principle that item-level external disagreement does not lower a catalog entry's confidence** (clinical effects stays `supported` despite item 10 vs Dupuy and item 14 vs Gregory & Bickel): **upheld.** A 17-item catalog of what the book reports is `supported` as a catalog. The item-level disputes are flagged against the items, which is the right place.

## Batch patterns (each is also in the rows)

A. **"Single-lab" applied to multi-source data.** Recruitment cites eight authors (1946-1967) and power cites two sources (Chikvadze 1961; Siff & Verkhoshansky 1999 figures), yet both entries say "single-lab". Thrown-load (Verkhoshansky 1977 alone) and depth-jump (Verkhoshansky's own series) may keep it.
B. **Unlabelled "When to apply" openers.** The criterion I applied to all 15: label "Inference:" only where the writer generalises beyond what the book itself recommends. Under that rule, power (generalises from two exercises to all SSC vs concentric exercises) and the safety heuristic (links ES sequencing to the book's commutative-law argument, which the book does not do for ES) need the label. Two-force, kinetic, depth-jump and clinical openers restate the authors' own recommendations and pass.
C. **Fixes that shifted the book's meaning.** "Apply the p.214 contraindications without exception" hardens "generally not advisable". "Do not use elastic-band resistance alone" softens "should not be used". Both are required.

New: Related calls Ratov's approach "contemporaneous Soviet". The book dates Reding to "the early 1970s" but gives no date for Siff's visit to Ratov's lab (p.208 says only that the techniques were "developed decades ago"). | C1 |

New: When NOT says "one reported duplication effort", but the page describes two attempts (a first "Unable to produce comparable results", then "again tried"). Filename slug still says "not-replicated" (note only: renaming breaks links; decide at promotion). | C2 |
| heuristic--nine-reasons-electrostimulation-research-conflicts.md | FIX | NEW PROBLEM (minor) | Items 7, 8, 9 fixed and match idx 221. New: (1) item 6 says no single study covered the parameter space "even in the more extensive review by Lloyd et al (1986)"; the book says the more extensive *studies* varied several parameters "as summarised in the thorough review by Lloyd et al", and no single study varied all. (2) Why it works: "not evidence for or against ES itself" and the five-way grouping are the writer's, unlabelled. | C3, C4 |

## Rulings on the fixer's "Disagreements with the review"

1. **Depth-jump `contested`: overruled; set `supported` (C17).** This is the criterion I apply to all three confidence questions, for this and later batches. An internal contradiction sets `contested` when it disputes the entry's title claim. When it touches only a secondary detail, it is recorded in the body. The p.222 contradiction ("diminishes sharply" vs "stabilise and do not increase any further") concerns only what happens past 1.15 m, and both readings agree that force does not rise past 1.15 m. The claim (optimal range 0.75-1.15 m, power at the low end, force at the high end) is stated once, consistently, and matches Fig 4.10. A `contested` label would tell a reader the range itself is disputed, which the book does not show. Keep both statements in the body.
2. **Thrown-load `contested`: upheld.** By the same criterion, the text-vs-figure disagreement concerns half of the title claim itself: whether a higher fall raises throw height. The text says it does; Fig 4.8a says it does only up to about 1-2 m for three of four loads. The reason is stated in the body. However, the title the fixer took from round 1 is false on the figure (C19).
3. **Fig 4.8b 13.3% curve**: the fixer's reading is correct (rises about 1.3 to about 2.0 near 15 J, then dips to about 1.8). Labelling the thin-arc identification Inference is correct; the 4x KE check above supports it.
4. **Fig 4.7 curve 1 peak "about 0.08-0.1 s"**: accepted.
5. **Ward & Shkuratova 2002 not cited**: accepted. Record as an unresolved spot: that abstract gives Kots's claimed gains as "up to 40%", against the book's "more than 20%" (p.209). Not a required change.
6. **Gregory & Bickel cited without journal**: accepted then. It is now confirmed, so C8 (optional) adds the journal and article type.
7. **MACS/MICS mainstream-status judgment left as Inference**: accepted. But the entry's `contested` still has no stated reason (C9).
8. **Fixer's principle that item-level external disagreement does not lower a catalog entry's confidence** (clinical effects stays `supported` despite item 10 vs Dupuy and item 14 vs Gregory & Bickel): **upheld.** A 17-item catalog of what the book reports is `supported` as a catalog. The item-level disputes are flagged against the items, which is the right place.

## Batch patterns (each is also in the rows)

A. **"Single-lab" applied to multi-source data.** Recruitment cites eight authors (1946-1967) and power cites two sources (Chikvadze 1961; Siff & Verkhoshansky 1999 figures), yet both entries say "single-lab". Thrown-load (Verkhoshansky 1977 alone) and depth-jump (Verkhoshansky's own series) may keep it.
B. **Unlabelled "When to apply" openers.** The criterion I applied to all 15: label "Inference:" only where the writer generalises beyond what the book itself recommends. Under that rule, power (generalises from two exercises to all SSC vs concentric exercises) and the safety heuristic (links ES sequencing to the book's commutative-law argument, which the book does not do for ES) need the label. Two-force, kinetic, depth-jump and clinical openers restate the authors' own recommendations and pass.
C. **Fixes that shifted the book's meaning.** "Apply the p.214 contraindications without exception" hardens "generally not advisable". "Do not use elastic-band resistance alone" softens "should not be used". Both are required.
